Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones

Marius Henry 1,3 &Michael Rizvi-Martel 2 &Michael Hahn 1 and 1 LaCoCo, Saarland University, Saarland Informatics Campus 2 Mila & Université de Montréal   3 Zuse School ELIZA
Abstract

Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind. Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation, which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution. On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation, which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones. These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers. We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off. In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size. Experiments support predictions of the theory.

1 Introduction

The success of large language models (LLMs) has prompted research into the learning and generalization properties of the underlying transformer architecture. Classical statistical learning theory provides a wealth of techniques that bound the generalization error as a function of the data size and the complexity of the hypothesis class. Recent work has brought these to bear on transformers (Covering numbers: Edelman et al. (2022); Trauger and Tewari (2024), Bayesian methods: Lintilhac and Shaikh (2026); Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026), VC Dimension: Yang et al. (2026c), inter alia). These results primarily address the i.i.d. regime – for transformers, this in particular implies that the test inputs are drawn from the same length distribution as the training inputs.

However, for transformer learning theory, the i.i.d. paradigm is arguably insufficient: it is highly desirable to understand when transformers can extrapolate to sequences longer than seen during training. This phenomenon is referred to as length-generalization (Bhattamishra et al., 2020; Anil et al., 2022; Kazemnejad et al., 2023, e.g.), and is understood to be diagnostic of when a transformer actually learns an underlying algorithmic solution, as opposed to length-dependent heuristics (Zhou et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026, e.g.). It also indicates when LLMs can be expected to perform a task reliably across long contexts (Jobanputra et al., 2025).

Length generalization is governed by two quantities: the number of training samples, and their length. Sample count determines how reliably the training data pins down the target function, as in classical statistical learning theory; sample length determines how well the model extrapolates, since the longest input length at which the target function’s behavior is observed dictates to which point a model will extrapolate beyond it. For a given target function and learning procedure, we thus need to consider not only its sample complexity (the required number of training samples), but also its length complexity (the required length of training samples).

Here, we take up the question of providing quantitative bounds on generalization along both axes for multi-layer transformers in the fixed-precision regime. We study the questions:

How do properties of a target function influence the length complexity and data complexity of the task?

When both sample size and length are bounded, how do they trade off? In particular, under a fixed token budget, how to best allocate sample size and length?

and address these by providing generalization bounds depending on both sample size and input length. The main idea is that training length determines which behaviors become observable; sample size determines how reliably those behaviors are learned. Below a task-dependent length threshold, some competing behaviors cannot be distinguished. Around the relevant transition, longer examples can make informative events much more common; increasing length can thus strongly reduce sample complexity in this regime. Beyond that transition, the benefit of additional length diminishes and additional independent examples matter more.

2 Background

2.1 Transformers

We study transformers in the fixed-precision regime, without positional encodings, as formalized by Li and Cotterell (2025); Li and Cotterell (2026) (see also Li et al. (2024); London and Kanade (2025)).

This class is expressive enough to accommodate key algorithmic primitives relevant to transformers, such as retrieving past symbols, checking global symbol alternation patterns, or the “induction head” construction. Fixed-precision transformers are less expressive than log- or unbounded-precision transformers; this turns out to be necessary for obtaining quantitative results, because length generalization bounds for the latter are known to be uncomputable in the worst case by results of Yang et al. (2026a). We discuss the detailed comparison across models of transformers in Appendix A.

Our model of transformers derives from Li and Cotterell (2025): we consider transformers with softmax attention, fixed precision, no positional encodings and strict causal masking. However, we generalize over Li and Cotterell (2025) in viewing transformers not as binary classifiers, but as providing an output at every position. We provide details in Appendix B.2. All activations are computed in 𝔽\mathbb{F}, a finite subset of ℝ\mathbb{R} extended with −∞-\infty and ∞\infty. The result of every operation is rounded to 𝔽\mathbb{F}.

Fix a finite alphabet Σ\Sigma. A fixed-precision transformer TT, also just called transformer consists of token embeddings in dimension DD, a sequence of LL layers each consisting of HH softmax attention heads with a ReLU feedforward network, and finally a linear output projection. Overall, it takes a word w∈Σ∗w\in\Sigma^{*} input and returns vectors of dimension ν\nu at every input position: T⁡(w)∈𝔽ν×|w|T(w)\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu\times|w|}. We suppose that HH always divides DD, and that the dimension per head DhD_{h} is uniform among the heads. We omit layer norm, as it is not essential to our results and requires extra care in fixed precision; see Appendix E.5 for more details. Assuming that Σ,𝔽\Sigma,\mathbb{F} and the output dimension ν\nu are shared, we refer to these transformers as ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(L,D,H)\mathcal{FPT}(L,D,H). See Appendix B.2 for details.

2.2 Learning framework

We follow prior sample complexity bounds in studying an idealized learning model that abstracts away from the algorithmic process of learning. Capacity-based learning bounds (Edelman et al., 2022; Trauger and Tewari, 2024; Yang et al., 2026c) apply to Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM), which finds parameters minimizing training error under some constraint on the hypothesis class. We contrast it with the Guess & Check algorithm (Chiang et al., 2023; Buzaglo et al., 2024, G&C, ), which samples parameter settings from the parameter space until a setting interpolating the training set is found. Guess & Check expands over ERM by modeling the inductive bias of SGD-like optimizers towards solutions occupying large volumes in parameter space (Chiang et al., 2023; Buzaglo et al., 2024). This is an important difference over bounds based on ERM (Edelman et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2026c; Trauger and Tewari, 2024), as it (i) allows us to explicitly take into account the effect of both the hypothesis class and the ground-truth function, (ii) while bounds depend more mildly on the hypothesis model’s size than capacity-based bounds. This enables stronger results when the target function can be represented by small models, and we find it to be borne out empirically in experiments. G&C is closely related to a Bayesian interpretation of learning, as it samples from a posterior over the parameter space conditional on the training set (Haussler et al., 1994, e.g.). We throughout work in the realizable regime, where the training data can be exactly fitted by an element of the hypothesis class. Here, ERM and G&C can be defined as follows:

Definition 2.1.

Let a hypothesis class ℋ=ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(Ls,Ds,Hs)\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{FPT}(L_{s},D_{s},H_{s}) (where “…s\dots{}_{s}” stands for “student”), and a training set (X(n),Y(n))n=1,…,N(X^{(n)},Y^{(n)})_{n=1,\dots,N}, be given.

The ERM Learner selects a transformer Ts∈ℋT_{s}\in\mathcal{H} such that TsT_{s} perfectly fits the training set: Ts​(X(n))≡Y(n)​∀(X(n),Y(n))n=1,…,NT_{s}(X^{(n)})\equiv Y^{(n)}\ \forall(X^{(n)},Y^{(n)})_{n=1,\dots,N}. The Guess & Check Learner returns a sample from the posterior

P⁡(Ts|Ts​(X(n))≡Y(n)​∀(X(n),Y(n))n=1,…,N)P\left(T_{s}\ |\ T_{s}(X^{(n)})\equiv Y^{(n)}\ \forall(X^{(n)},Y^{(n)})_{n=1,\dots,N}\right) (1)

where P⁡(Ts)P(T_{s}) is the uniform distribution over ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Intuitively, G&C adds an inductive bias towards hypotheses represented by a larger volume in parameter space. See Appendix A for discussion beyond the interpolating regime.

Remark 2.1.

Throughout this paper, we consider the student–teacher learning framework between two transformers TsT_{s} and TtT_{t}, with Ls≥Lt,Ds≥DtL_{s}\geq L_{t},D_{s}\geq D_{t}, Hs≥HtH_{s}\geq H_{t} and Dh,s≥Dh,tD_{h,s}\geq D_{h,t} for realizability.

3 Length Generalization

We first derive length generalization bounds when unbounded data samples are available (Section 3.1); and statistical generalization bounds at a fixed length (Section 4.1). We then derive joint generalization bounds (Section 4.2).

3.1 Deterministic Length Generalization

Our first result states that, if two fixed-precision transformers exactly agree up to a certain length bound CC, they must agree everywhere. We in fact obtain two distinct bounds with different rates:

This statement yields a first length generalization guarantee, in the setting where unbounded data samples are available: In this case, if a learned model TsT_{s} exactly fits data representing a target function expressed by TtT_{t} up to length CC, then we know Ts≡TtT_{s}\equiv T_{t} even on longer length strings, i.e., length generalization occurs.

See Appendix D for the formal proof; here, we provide an informal discussion to build intuition. Given a teacher transformer TtT_{t} implementing the target function and a student TsT_{s} from the hypothesis class, we introduce the difference function, which checks for any given word if the output vectors of both transformers match at every position. Previously, Li and Cotterell (2025) showed that fixed-precision transformers with a binary classifying output layer are expressively equivalent to LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], a fragment of linear temporal logic, and further can be represented as a partially-ordered deterministic finite automaton (poDFA) (Figure 2). A poDFA is a DFA where the reachability relation defines a partial order on the state set; intuitively, such automata have no nontrivial loops. Intuitively, the state space describes the dynamic of the transformer’s KV-cache; as soon as some activation is added to the KV-cache, it cannot be removed anymore, giving rise to the partially ordered loop-free structure.

Building on this, we express the difference function between the student and the teacher as a logic formula in LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], from which we obtain a poDFA 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta}. The student and the teacher transformers produce a different output somewhere on a word w1​…,wnw_{1}\dots,w_{n} if and only if 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta}, run on the word, ends up in the unique absorbing disagreement state ⊥\bot (Figure 2(e)). As a supplement, we mention in Appendix C, D how transformers exist as ordered Mealy machines (Def. C.5), providing a similar underlying ordered structure on individual transformers, even outside of the learning framework.

We then upper-bound the height of 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} – i.e., the length of its longest transition chain. The key idea here is that observing behaviour on strings up to roughly this length should be important for length generalization, because strings of this length should be minimally required to be able to observe the whole state space of 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} – and thus the whole range of behaviour expressed by the student and teacher models. We obtain C0,C1C_{0},C_{1} as two upper bounds on the height of 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} (eq. 2); whichever bound is smaller provides a tighter bound in a given setting, though neither dominates the other globally. Notably, we show some kind of tightness in LL and 𝔽\mathbb{F} of our bounds in Appendix D.5, where we prove that any upper bound on the height must depends at least linearly on |𝔽||\mathbb{F}| and LL.

Now, if TsT_{s} and TtT_{t} agree up to length C=min⁡{C0,C1}C=\min\{C_{0},C_{1}\}, 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} cannot visit a ⊥\bot state on any word of this length. But given that CC upper-bounds the height of the automaton, the ⊥\bot state cannot be reachable even by longer inputs, and Ts≡TtT_{s}\equiv T_{t} across Σ∗\Sigma^{*}.

The above entails a first length-generalization bound in the limiting case where all data up to some length is available; it is an illustrative first special case of our general result.

3.2 Extension to the probabilistic framework

We next ask for a similar length generalization guarantee when TsT_{s} and TtT_{t} are equal only on most strings up to length KK. Setting the data distribution 𝒟K:=Unif⁡(Σ≤K)\mathcal{D}_{K}:=\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{\leq K}) and using the bound CC from Lemma 3.1, we indeed find a probabilistic extension of the guarantee:

See Appendix D.4 for the formal proof. Intuitively, this holds for two reasons: (i) the poDFA 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} ultimately reaches a sink absorbing state; (ii) the input distribution 𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{K} is uniform and so are the letters: this implies that for any non-absorbing state, the probability to leave the state by reading the next letter is at least of 1/|Σ|1/|\Sigma|. Therefore, after a big enough number of steps KK, 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} will be likely to live in an absorbing state. In particular, since the probability of a transition is at least 1/|Σ|1/|\Sigma|, the overall probability of a word to reach an absorbing state after KK steps dominates the binomial law Y∼Bin⁡(K,1/|Σ|)Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(K,1/|\Sigma|). The lemma follows from the application of a Chernoff bound.

4 Joining Length and Statistical Generalization

4.1 Data complexity

We lift the deterministic statement to a statistical generalization statement. The key here is to combine Lemma 3.1 with statistical in-distribution generalization on the strings up to length KK:

Note here that 𝒪⁡(⋅)\mathcal{O}(\cdot) absorbs constants depending on 𝔽\mathbb{F} and ν\nu. The ERM bound has a similar flavor to bounds using capacity-based arguments (Edelman et al., 2022; Trauger and Tewari, 2024; Yang et al., 2026c) in that it scales with parameters count of the hypothesis class. The G&C bound has a similar dependency but scales with Ds​DtD_{s}D_{t} rather than Ds2D_{s}^{2}. This provides improved generalization when a large student network learns a low-complexity target.

This result extends the work of Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026) with some improvements; we give the exact values of BB and BE​R​MB_{ERM} and discuss the proof and extensions in Appendix E. For ERM, this is a straightforward application of Appendix B.1 in Buzaglo et al. (2024). For G&C, the proof strategy (Appendix E) is to show that low-complexity teachers can be embedded in many equivalent ways into the parameter space of a higher-complexity hypothesis class; this means that G&C is intrinsically more likely to find low-complexity interpolators. This insight (Buzaglo et al. (2024)) drives the appearance of a teacher complexity term, and a milder dependence on student complexity than based on hypothesis class parameter count alone.

4.2 Main Result: Joint Statistical and Length Generalization

We now combine length and statistical generalization to obtain our main result. The basic intuition is that generalization occurs when (i) the length is sufficiently long so that all representative behavior relevant at long lengths are already visible, (ii) the sample size is sufficient for achieving low test error at this length; combining (i) and (ii) then entails low test error at higher lengths. The result is:

See Appendix F.1 for the formal proof. For ERM, an analogous result ensues from bounding NN appropriately, following Proposition 4.1. In addition, the theorem can be adapted to alternative distributions D~K\widetilde{D}_{K} if they sample enough long words; we give an example in Appendix F.4.

4.3 Tradeoff between Length and Data Complexity

The previous theorem provides conditions on the data complexity NN and the training length threshold KK, such that low loss can be achieved. Assuming the same learning framework for student TsT_{s}, teacher TtT_{t} and writing s≔|Σ|s\coloneqq|\Sigma|, we now investigate how these quantities trade off, by giving an error bound for any joint choice of NN and KK:

See Appendix F.2 for the proof. This value aC​(K)a_{C}(K) lower-bounds the probability of reaching an absorbing state by time KK, and aC​(K)=0a_{C}(K)=0 when K<CK<C. This theorem holds for either of the Guess & Check or the ERM learner, setting BB accordingly following Proposition 4.1. Moreover, under an appropriate definition of aC​(K)a_{C}(K), the theorem even remains valid if the input strings are generated from appropriate nonuniform distributions (Appendix G.2). We further complement the upper bound (10) with a lower bound: there are families of target functions and input distributions such that the expected test error on long inputs is lower-bounded by B8​N​aC​(K)\frac{B}{8Na_{C}(K)} for an appropriate choice of BB (Appendix, Theorem G.3).

Takeaway: Importance of Long Training Samples for Transformers.

This implies the following: First, when K<CK<C, there is no assurance of length generalization. Second, when KK just slightly exceeds CC, length generalization can be guaranteed, but only at an extraordinary sample size on the order of ⪆sC\gtrapprox s^{C}, with ss the size of the alphabet. Namely, aC​(C)=s−Ca_{C}(C)=s^{-C}, leading to a sample size requirement Nr​e​q​(C)=N0​sCN_{req}(C)=N_{0}s^{C} where N0=ρ​BδϵN_{0}=\frac{\rho B_{\delta}}{\epsilon}. Intuitively, this happens because only a small fraction of the samples will already have reached an absorbing state; most samples will thus not be informative about the target function’s behavior on long strings.

Third, increasing KK by a constant can reduce the required sample size by a multiplicative factor. Specifically, increasing length from CC to s​CsC reduces the required sample size by a factor of at least sC/2s^{C}/2; a linear increase of KK permits an exponential saving on NN.

Given a fixed training-token budget B​u​d​g​e​t=N​KBudget=NK, the above considerations allow us to determine an optimal allocation to NN and KK; we show in Appendix F.3 that, for C≥2C\geq 2, the following closed form achieves an error bound within a factor 1+𝒪⁡(log⁡C/C)1+\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log C/C}) of the optimum:

K^≔⌈|Σ|​(C+log⁡C+log2⁡C+2​C​log⁡C)⌉,\widehat{K}\coloneqq\left\lceil|\Sigma|\left(C+\log C+\sqrt{\log^{2}C+2C\log C}\right)\right\rceil,

provided B​u​d​g​e​t≥K^Budget\geq\widehat{K}. Intuitively, this means that close-to-optimal budget allocation can be achieved at around K∼|Σ|​CK\sim|\Sigma|C, exponentially more efficient than at K∼CK\sim C.

Our result reveals that there are several regimes of generalization. When KK is too small, there is in general no hope of length generalization no matter how large NN is. When KK has just crossed the threshold given by the longest chain, one may need a very large NN, because only few strings will have reached the final state. In this regime, increasing KK further is much more efficient than increasing NN: increasing KK by an additive constant can cut down NN by a multiplicative factor.

4.4 Extension with Local Attention

Local attention has emerged as an effective and popular addition to transformers (Beltagy et al., 2020, e.g.). It is also relevant because positional information often specifically introduces a locality bias favoring attention to recent position (Press et al., 2022; Su et al., 2024). Local attention thus simultaneously serves as a simplified account of the role of positional information (similar to positional functions in Limit Transformers, Huang et al. (2025a); Izzo et al. (2025)). In each layer, we add a certain number of local attention heads at some window size WW; for these heads, context positions at distance >W>W are masked. Both WW and the number of local heads are hyperparameters. We refer to Li and Cotterell (2026) for the full formalization in the ℱ​𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{FPT} context.

Formally, we can model an ℱ​𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{FPT} with local attention in terms of a more complex automaton that arises as a cascade product of a poDFA with a simple automaton that maintains the last L⋅WL\cdot W symbols. That is, we can model the difference automaton 𝒜\mathcal{A} in terms of the cascade product of a poDFA representing the output difference between the two transformers with a simple automaton that maintains the last L⋅WL\cdot W symbols. More details in Appendix G.1.

The statistical generalization guarantee (Proposition 4.1) is unaffected, because the number of parameters does not change when making some heads local. The length generalization guarantee changes. First, the construction we provide is only valid for the bound C0C_{0} in Eq. 2. Second this threshold C0C_{0} receives a factor of R≔W​L+1R\coloneqq WL+1. Third, the bounding binomial probability to go forward in the underlying poDFA is also reduced from |Σ|−1|\Sigma|^{-1} to |Σ|−R|\Sigma|^{-R}. Thus, as long as WW is fixed, we have the same qualitative predictions as above: model size impacts data and length complexity; and sample size and length trade off.

5 Experiments

We introduce three families of tasks, and study (i) the impact of teacher and student complexity on length and data complexity, and (ii) the predicted interaction between length and sample size.

Tasks.

We defined three task families, each along a complexity scale indexed by k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, as follows (i) Alternating languages LkL_{k}: Detecting whether ≥k\geq k distinct blocks of aa’s and bb’s have occurred (Yang et al., 2025a) – that is, checking membership in the languages L2=a+​b+​Σ∗;L3=a+​b+​a+​Σ∗L_{2}=a^{+}b^{+}\Sigma^{*};L_{3}=a^{+}b^{+}a^{+}\Sigma^{*}, etc. There is a teacher family with number of layers Lk=Θ⁡(k)L_{k}=\Theta(k), embedding dimension Dk=O⁡(1)D_{k}=O(1), head count Hk=O⁡(1)H_{k}=O(1) and fixed alphabet size |Σ|k=O⁡(1)|\Sigma|_{k}=O(1). Specifically, the letter sampling is not uniform, with probability to alternate block set to 0.050.05. This still fits our theoretical framework, as explained in Appendix H.1.1. (ii) Alphabet languages AkA_{k}: Detecting whether all symbols from a given alphabet Σk=[k]\Sigma_{k}=[k] have occurred. There is a teacher family with Lk=O⁡(1)L_{k}=O(1), Dk=O⁡(k)D_{k}=O(k), Hk=O⁡(k)H_{k}=O(k), |Σ|k=O⁡(k)|\Sigma|_{k}=O(k). (iii) Induction Head tasks 𝐼𝐻k\mathit{IH}_{k}: Outputting which next tokens can follow the current token under the context’s bigram distribution over the alphabet Σk=[k]\Sigma_{k}=[k] (Edelman et al., 2024, cf.); that is, given the current token α\alpha output a vector ∈𝔽|Σ|\in\mathbb{F}^{|\Sigma|} indicating for which symbols β\beta the bigram α​β\alpha\beta has contextually occurred. There is a teacher family with Lk=O⁡(1)L_{k}=O(1), Dk=O⁡(k)D_{k}=O(k), Hk=O⁡(1)H_{k}=O(1), |Σ|k=O⁡(k)|\Sigma|_{k}=O(k), with local attention. See Appendix H for teacher constructions. Taken together, these tasks allow us to test the theoretical prediction that the teacher size (impacted by LL, HH, DD, |Σ||\Sigma|) impacts both length and data complexity.

Setup.

To test our predictions against ordinary gradient-based training, we train FP32 transformers with Adam Kingma and Ba (2014) and binary cross-entropy over 1010 seeds. We use binary classification because exact logit-equality in FP32 is not realistic. The difference function between the student and the teacher then checks for logit signs rather than exact values (Appendix H.2). In addition, we retain only runs with perfect training accuracy—that is, runs that correctly classify every supervised target on every training word. This enforces the interpolation conditioning of Guess & Check. Trained architectural sizes are fixed and common across a family, unless explicitly varied. When sweeping NN, we adjust KK across tasks to match the fraction of words exhibiting the required blocks, letters, or bigrams, making examples approximately comparable in informativeness (Appendix H.2). Sweeps of KK instead compare tasks at common lengths.

Effect of Transformers Size on Data and Length Complexity.

Across the three families, increasing teacher size impacts the sample size NN and training length KK at which generalization becomes successful (Figure 4). This is in line with our theoretical predictions, in particular, the G&C-based bounds. Interestingly, the student size had relatively small impact on sample size and length (Appendix H.3.2). Thus, G&C-based bounds are successful in capturing the fact teacher size is an important factor beyond student size, but may still be overly pessimistic about the impact of student size.

Tradeoff between Sample Size and Length.

Longer training words can substantially reduce the sample size needed for generalization (Figure 5). In particular, we find the non-linear interaction between the two quantities, qualitatively in line with the predictions from Figure 3. This backs the idea that an efficient token-budget allocation should ensure that training samples are long enough. See Appendix H.3.3 for further results showing the same pattern.

6 Discussion

Our result goes beyond established theory in two ways: First, it goes beyond statistical generalization bounds for transformers by guaranteeing length generalization. Prior learning results for transformers characterize generalization error and sample size when the test and train samples are at the same sequence length (Edelman et al., 2022; Trauger and Tewari, 2024; Li et al., 2026; Truong, 2024; Yang et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2025; Rizvi-Martel et al., 2026; Lintilhac and Shaikh, 2026; Mousavi-Hosseini et al., 2025; Hanneke et al., 2026; Joshi et al., 2025). Our results instead consider the more general case of length generalization, in the setting of fixed-precision transformers. We note that our main result ingests the statistical generalization bound essentially as a black box; hence, our results might analogously also be formalized on the basis of other statistical generalization bounds.

Second, our results go beyond prior work on length generalization by giving explicit and joint rates for sample size and length. So far, the most generally predictive account of length generalization has been the RASP-L Conjecture (Zhou et al., 2024) and its formalization via C-RASP and Limit Transformers (Huang et al., 2025a). This theory has been highly predictive of which tasks empirically show length generalization (Yang et al., 2026b), but provides no quantitative predictions. Notably, C-RASP is more powerful than ℱ​𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{FPT}; e.g. it can model the MAJORITY language. However, C-RASP is a too loose target for quantitive learning bounds: Yang et al. (2026a) show that, beyond the shallow-depth case (Izzo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), any length threshold would need to grow uncomputably with model complexity. The positive fragment C-RASP+ has expressivity equivalent to fixed-precision transformers and was studied in Yang et al. (2026a); Zetzsche et al. (2026). We compare with these results in detail in Appendix A. Importantly, our work innovates over these prior results by providing joint generalization guarantees in both sample size and length.

Like capacity-based generalization bounds (Edelman et al., 2022; Trauger and Tewari, 2024; Yang et al., 2026c), our work treats an idealized learning model that abstracts away from the computational process of finding a model fitting the training data. Understanding optimization dynamics for transformers has been difficult. Progress has been made for specific task families and restricted models, such as single layers (Yang et al., 2025b; Mwigo and Dasgupta, 2026; Huang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024, e.g.) (including one-layer models performing chain-of-thought, Huang et al. (2025b)) or specific task families (Nichani et al., 2024, e.g.). We view the study of G&C as an (imperfect) proxy for part of the implicit inductive bias of SGD-like learning; understanding of optimization dynamics for a general multi-layer model and a general hypothesis class will require new methods.

The main limitation of our results is that they predict asymptotic rates but not yet concrete realistic numerical bounds for specific tasks and models. The primary barrier here is that the bounds involve large constants involving the fixed-precision set 𝔽\mathbb{F}, which is large at full-precision training. It is an interesting question whether realistic numerical bounds can be obtained when training with strong quantization. Further limitations are that fixed-precision transformers are less expressive than log-precision or infinite-precision transformers, we did not treat positional encodings, and studied G&C and ERM as opposed to optimization dynamics.

7 Conclusion

We have provided generalization bounds for multi-layer fixed-precision transformers that account for the roles of both the number and the length of training samples. We provided a joint treatment of both dimensions, showing that, under a given token budget, increasing length can sometimes be exponentially more efficient than increasing sample size.

Appendix A FAQ

  1. 1.

    How do the results relate to Yang et al. (2026a); Zetzsche et al. (2026)?

    Yang et al. (2026a) give two core results: (i) an impossibility result for computable length generalization bounds for C-RASP, and (ii) a deterministic length generalization bound analogous to our Lemma 3.1 for C-RASP+\text{C-RASP}^{+}.

    The first result indicates that C-RASP is too powerful a target for obtaining quantitative learning results for transformers: even though C-RASP has been successful in predicting generalization behaviour experimentally (Huang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2026b), there are C-RASP-expressible tasks where training data would need to include strings with astronomically large lengths. Yang et al. (2026a); Zetzsche et al. (2026) further show an analogue of our Lemma 3.1 for C-RASP+\text{C-RASP}^{+}, the positive fragment of C-RASP, giving a computable bound in the size of the defining C-RASP formula. Most recently, Zetzsche et al. (2026) have further studied the role of sample size. They show exponential sample size bounds for C-RASP+\text{C-RASP}^{+} and another fragment, called C-RASP1\text{C-RASP}_{1}.

    C-RASP+\text{C-RASP}^{+} has the same expressivity as fixed-precision transformers, though there is no direct 1-to-1 link between the transformer size parameters (LL, DD, HH) and the size of defining C-RASP+ formulas. As a consequence, length and sample complexities that we obtain may not be directly comparable to bounds obtained for C-RASP+\text{C-RASP}^{+} in Yang et al. (2026a); Zetzsche et al. (2026).

    An important difference of our results, besides directly applying to a transformer model rather than the C-RASP+ logic, is that we obtain joint bounds allowing us to understand the tradeoff between sample length and sample size.

  2. 2.

    How do the experiments differ from the theoretical learning model? What are the implications of these differences?

    The point of our experiments is to test theoretical predictions (obtained for idealized learners G&C or ERM on fixed-precision transformers) in a realistic training setup using gradient-based optimization (Adam) on high-precision (FP32) transformers. Whereas the theoretical setup asks for exact match of the output vectors, the experiments instead train for per-dimension binary cross-entropy. In experiments, we select only runs with perfect training accuracy, enforcing interpolation, as assumed in theory.

  3. 3.

    Why study fixed-precision transformers? Why not study C-RASP / Limit Transformers?

    It is a well-established empirical finding that transformers show strong length generalization on the class of languages expressed by fixed-precision transformers (Li and Cotterell, 2025; Yang et al., 2026b). They are thus a natural target for joint treatment of sample and length complexity.

    Fixed-precision transformers define a strict subset of C-RASP (Yang and Chiang, 2024) and Limit Transformers (Huang et al., 2025a; Izzo et al., 2025). On the one hand, there is empirical evidence that transformers also show length generalization on tasks that are expressible in C-RASP but not by fixed-precision transformers, such as MAJORITY or certain regular languages such as bounded-depth Dyck languages (Yang et al., 2026b), which require a transformer’s numerical precision to grow with the input length. On the other hand, as discussed above, Yang et al. (2026a) show that C-RASP cannot admit computable length generalization bounds, i.e., any threshold CC satisfying (3) for all of C-RASP must grow faster in the size of the C-RASP formula (or Limit Transformer) than any computable function. This indicates that C-RASP is too broad as a target for quantitative length generalization bounds (Yang et al., 2026a; Zetzsche et al., 2026). It is an interesting question for future work whether tractable generalization bounds exist for some natural class between fixed-precision transformers and C-RASP.

  4. 4.

    How do the results relate to Izzo et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025)?

    Izzo et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025) provide quantitative length generalization bounds for C-RASP or Limit Transformers fragments with only one or two layers. On the one hand, fixed-precision transformers form a strict subset of C-RASP/Limit Transformers; on the other hand, our results apply to the multi-layer setup, where computable quantitative bounds for C-RASP are impossible (see Items 1 and 3).

  5. 5.

    The paper studies ERM and G&C. Why not study optimizers like SGD or Adam?

    Our work follows prior work (Edelman et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2025; Izzo et al., 2025; Trauger and Tewari, 2024, e.g.) in studying idealized learners abstracting away from gradient dynamics. ERM in particular is a highly popular standard approach for deriving learning bounds. Guess-and-check models the inductive bias of realistic training towards solutions occupying high volume in parameter space (Buzaglo et al., 2024), unlike ERM. Prior and concurrent work has provided evidence that parameter space volume is useful for understanding transformer generalization, finding that certain hard-to-learn functions occupy small volume in parameter space (Hahn and Rofin, 2024; Kövér et al., 2026; Zhu and Chiang, 2026); G&C is consistent with this by predicting easier generalization for functions occupying high parameter space volume. Neither G&C nor ERM should be considered full models of learning. For instance, for matrix factorization, Alexander et al. (2025) show that SGD can in some cases of matrix factorization generalize even better than G&C. Understanding gradient dynamics for general mutli-layer transformers is extremely difficult. Developing quantitative generalization bounds for gradient-based training is a major task for future work; the 1-layer setup might be a tractable starting point.

  6. 6.

    Could the framework be extended to handle positional encodings?

    Prior bounds for statistical generalization (not length generalization) of transformers use fixed absolute positional encodings (Edelman et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2026c; Lintilhac and Shaikh, 2026). That would also be possible to include in our setup, though one would need to understand their effects on the automaton structure. Learnable absolute positional encodings are harder to account for as they lead to rapid growth of the parameter count with the input length (as acknowledged by Edelman et al. (2022)), and are inherently undefined outside of the training length range. Huang et al. (2025a) impose translation invariance constraints to constrain the hypothesis space in their analysis.

    Relative positional encodings can be easier to account for, as they do not involve an unbounded number of parameters. Yang et al. (2025a) show that ALiBi (Press et al., 2022) can be understood (in the context of C-RASP) as the addition of local predicates; we expect the effect on fixed-precision transformers to be very similar to the effect provided by local attention. We opt to analyze local attention, as it is nowadays popular in LLM design and has been rigorously formalized in the fixed-precision setup by Li and Cotterell (2026). RoPE (Su et al., 2024) is harder to capture theoretically in the context of length generalization: while it can be formalized in terms of modular predicates (Yang et al., 2025a) (which admit exact automata-theoretic treatment in an appropriate extension of our poDFA framework, with appropriate modifications to the length complexity term), this does not characterize conventional RoPE implementation, which rather behave like fixed-length backwards-lookup operators (Jerad et al., 2026), and may in fact impair empirical length generalization (Jerad et al., 2026).

  7. 7.

    Can the theory predict specific numerical bounds?

    Our aim is to predict qualitative rates and the shape of the tradeoff between sample size and input length. Predicting numerical bounds faces the challenge that constants depending on the precision set 𝔽\mathbb{F} will be extremely large at full-precision training. Constants involving it are in general needed (Appendix D.5). It is a highly interesting (and challenging) problem for future work to make bounds numerically tighter.

  8. 8.

    Are the teacher constructions for the three task families minimal?

    For the Alternation Languages, Yang et al. (2025a) show that transformer depth for LkL_{k} must be ≥k\geq k under a more expressive formalization of transformers (fixed-precision residual stream, unbounded-precision attention). Thus, our teacher family with Lk=Θ⁡(k),Dk=O⁡(1),Hk=O⁡(1)L_{k}=\Theta(k),D_{k}=O(1),H_{k}=O(1) is optimal up to rates.

    For the Alphabet Languages, we found models hard to train when head count was <k<k, though we do not have a proof that an ℱ​𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{FPT} requires Ω⁡(k)\Omega(k) heads. However, a simple information-theoretic argument shows that Dk⋅|𝔽|=Ω⁡(log⁡k)D_{k}\cdot|\mathbb{F}|=\Omega(\log k) is unavoidable; hence, the teachers do need to grow with kk. For the Induction Head Languages, the same argument applies as k→∞k\rightarrow\infty.

  9. 9.

    Why are there missing points in some experimental plots?

    As detailed in Appendix H.2, across all configurations, each run over 10 random seeds, we strictly retain only the runs that achieve 100% training accuracy, consistent with the Guess & Check conditioning assumption. Notably, we observe in Figure 8 that Alternating languages LkL_{k} can’t reach 100% training accuracy when the trained student has less than k−1k-1 layers, as expected (Yang et al. (2025a)). Similarly, students learning from Alphabet languages AkA_{k} with head count Hs<kH_{s}<k struggle to fit the training data (Figure 10).

  10. 10.

    What is strict causal masking? Why assume it?

    Strict causal masking means that attention heads cannot attend to the query position, but only to strictly preceding positions. Strict causal masking increases expressivity compared to non-strict causal masking (Li and Cotterell, 2025). We believe that our techniques and main results would equally apply in the non-strict-masking setup, though then applying to a less expressive model and correspondingly a smaller class of functions.

  11. 11.

    The theoretical bounds include effects of both teacher size (the transformer representing the target function) and the student size (the transformers in the learner’s hypothesis class). Experiments show strong effects of the teacher but weak effects for the student. Why?

    Our theoretical predictions provide worst-case sufficient upper bounds on the test error; practical learning outcomes may be better both because the theoretical analysis may not be tight and because gradient-based learning may generalize better than the theoretical idealizations ERM and G&C. Indeed, it is a common observation that key techniques for proving statistical learning bounds show an overly pessimistic dependency on the student size: overparameterized neural networks often generalize very well, far better than is accounted for by capacity-based bounds that guarantee learning for ERM via uniform convergence (Nagarajan and Kolter, 2019; Zhang et al., 2017; Bartlett et al., 2021, e.g.). The G&C analysis as developed by Buzaglo et al. (2024), that we adopt in Section 4.1, goes some way towards ameliorating this, as its dependence on the student size is substantially milder than for the capacity-based ERM bounds. Some work has provided generalization bounds that scale very mildly in the student size for simpler neural networks (Allen-Zhu et al., 2019; Arora et al., 2019, e.g.), though the extension of such results to transformers will likely require new techniques.

  12. 12.

    The bound CC on the height of the difference automata is chosen as the minimum of two bounds (Lemma 3.1). When is which bound stronger? What do we know about tightness?

    C0C_{0} involves the layer count, hidden dimension, and per-head dimension of both student and teacher; it is exponential in the per-head dimension and linear in the others. C1C_{1} involves only the student layer count and the alphabet size; it is exponential in either and becomes polynomial in LsL_{s} when the alphabet is fixed. Importantly, CC is the minimum both, i.e., our results always apply to the smaller of both bounds. Thus, even if our theorems were stated just for C:=C0C:=C_{0} or C:=C1C:=C_{1}, they would remain valid; giving two versions strengthens our results.

    The two bounds have strengths in different hyperparameter regimes. In the regime where models are very deep, C0C_{0} is asymptotically smaller, and CC remains linear in LsL_{s} and LtL_{t}. In the regime where models are very wide, C1C_{1} is asymptotically smaller, as it does not depend on the hidden dimension. The exception is when the number of heads also increases: then, the per-head dimension Dh,sD_{h,s} decreases, and C0C_{0} may become more favorable.

    Notably, only two quantities enter both bounds: LL and |𝔽||\mathbb{F}|; both bounds additionally require other quantities, but they can trade off which each other; e.g., as discussed above, taking into account DD can turn the depth dependence from exponential (in C1C_{1}) to linear (in C0C_{0}). We show the unavoidability of including the two quantities LL and |𝔽||\mathbb{F}| in Appendix D.5.

Appendix B Conventions and Background

We specify the fixed-precision transformer model used throughout the paper, following Li and Cotterell (2025, Section 3 and Appendix B). Our main adaptations are that we retain the number of attention heads explicitly and that we drop layer norm as well as the attention score normalization (see Appendix E.5 for more). In addition, we distinguish tokenwise vectorial outputs from their word-level binary satisfaction framework.

B.1 Fixed-precision arithmetic

Fixed-precision set.

A fixed-precision set or finite-precision set 𝔽\mathbb{F} is a finite ordered set, constructed from a subset of the real numbers 𝔽fin\mathbb{F}_{\mathrm{fin}} containing 00 and 11, and extended with the two infinite limits:

𝔽=𝔽fin∪{−∞,+∞},{0,1}⊆𝔽fin⊂ℝ,p≔|𝔽|.\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_{\mathrm{fin}}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\},\qquad\{0,1\}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{\mathrm{fin}}\subset\mathbb{R},\qquad p\coloneqq|\mathbb{F}|. (11)

The set 𝔽\mathbb{F} is equipped with deterministic rules for rounding every elementary operation back to 𝔽\mathbb{F}, including overflow and underflow. When we study transformers on a fixed-precision set 𝔽\mathbb{F}, all scalar parameters and intermediate calculation values must belong to 𝔽\mathbb{F}. The precision convention is fixed and independent of the input length.

We use the natural extended-real rules whenever defined, in particular

exp(−∞)=0,exp(+∞)=+∞,f/(±∞)=0(f∈𝔽fin).\exp(-\infty)=0,\qquad\exp(+\infty)=+\infty,\qquad f/(\pm\infty)=0\quad(f\in\mathbb{F}_{\mathrm{fin}}).

More details about the edge cases stemming from the finite-precision arithmetic can be found in Li and Cotterell (2025).

B.2 Transformers

Transformers read words w=w1⋯wn∈Σ∗w=w_{1}\cdots w_{n}\in\Sigma^{*} directly; throughout, n=|w|n=|w| refers to the length of an input word. Differently to Li and Cotterell (2025), no end-of-sequence token is appended and transformer computations are performed only at the ordinary positions 1,…,n1,\ldots,n. This allows for a broader definition of transformers, with vectorial outputs at every position.

We use i,ji,j for positions, ℓ\ell for layers, dd for the vectorial dimension and hh for heads.

Definition B.1 (Fixed-precision transformer).

Fix a depth L≥0L\geq 0, a width D≥1D\geq 1, and a number of heads H≥1H\geq 1 with H|DH\mid D; put Dh=D/HD_{h}=D/H. A fixed-precision transformer assigns to each w∈Σ∗w\in\Sigma^{*} of length nn an output

T⁡(w)∈𝔽ν×n.T(w)\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu\times n}.

It consists of a token embedding, LL transformer blocks, and a pointwise output layer. Thus T(w):,i∈𝔽νT(w)_{:,i}\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu} is defined at every ordinary position 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. We use ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(L,D,H)\mathcal{FPT}(L,D,H) for the class of such transformers with the corresponding parameter sizes.

Remark.

All calculations below use the fixed-precision convention of Definition B.1.

Embedding.

A map e:Σ→𝔽De:\Sigma\to\mathbb{F}^{D} determines the 00-th layer Λ(0)\Lambda^{(0)}, with

Λ(0)(w)∈𝔽D×n,Λ:,i(0)(w)=e(wi)(1≤i≤n).\Lambda^{(0)}(w)\in\mathbb{F}^{D\times n},\qquad\Lambda^{(0)}_{:,i}(w)=e(w_{i})\quad(1\leq i\leq n). (12)

There are no positional encodings.

For 0≤ℓ<L0\leq\ell<L and 1≤h≤H1\leq h\leq H, we define the attention mechanism of head hh with input Λ(ℓ)∈𝔽D×n\Lambda^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{F}^{D\times n}. We sometimes omit ℓ\ell and hh from the notation for readability purposes.

Attention.

An attention mechanism is a map Ah:𝔽D×n→𝔽Dh×n\operatorname{A}_{h}:\mathbb{F}^{D\times n}\to\mathbb{F}^{D_{h}\times n}. First, choose WQ,WK,WV∈𝔽Dh×DW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{F}^{D_{h}\times D} and set

Q=WQ​Λ(ℓ),K=WK​Λ(ℓ),V=WV​Λ(ℓ).Q=W_{Q}\Lambda^{(\ell)},\qquad K=W_{K}\Lambda^{(\ell)},\qquad V=W_{V}\Lambda^{(\ell)}. (13)

The attention mechanism has a strict causal masking: the visible positions at ii are {1,…,i−1}\{1,\ldots,i-1\}. For 1≤j<i1\leq j<i, compute the attention score

Si,j:=Q:,i𝖳K:,j.S_{i,j}:=Q_{:,i}^{\mathsf{T}}K_{:,j}. (14)

For a given position ii, we consider the maximum of queried attention scores at position i maxi:=maxj<i⁡Si,j\max_{i}:=\max_{j<i}S_{i,j} and define the stabilized attention weights

αi,j:=exp⁡(Si,j−maxi)∑k<iexp⁡(Si,k−maxi).\alpha_{i,j}:=\frac{\exp(S_{i,j}-\max_{i})}{\sum_{k<i}\exp(S_{i,k}-\max_{i})}.

The attention map is consequently defined as

Ah(Λ(ℓ)):,i:=∑j<iαi,jV:,j.\operatorname{A}_{h}(\Lambda^{(\ell)})_{:,i}:=\sum_{j<i}\alpha_{i,j}V_{:,j}.

As there is no well-defined attention score for the first index i=1i=1, we set Ah(Λ(ℓ)):,1:=𝟎∈𝔽Dh\operatorname{A}_{h}(\Lambda^{(\ell)})_{:,1}:=\mathbf{0}\in\mathbb{F}^{D_{h}}.

We define by extension the head-agnostic attention mechanism A(ℓ)\operatorname{A}^{(\ell)} as the concatenation of the attention heads, with

A:,i(ℓ)(Λ(ℓ)):=(A1(Λ(ℓ)):,i𝖳,…,AH(Λ(ℓ)):,i𝖳)𝖳.\operatorname{A}^{(\ell)}_{:,i}(\Lambda^{(\ell)}):=\left(\operatorname{A}_{1}(\Lambda^{(\ell)})_{:,i}^{\mathsf{T}},...,\operatorname{A}_{H}(\Lambda^{(\ell)})_{:,i}^{\mathsf{T}}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}.

For each intermediate sublayer Λ(ℓ+0.5),0≤ℓ<L\Lambda^{(\ell+0.5)},0\leq\ell<L, we define a position-wise feed-forward mechanism applied to this sublayer. We consider feed-forwards with one hidden layer of dimension DffD_{\mathrm{ff}}. We set Dff=DD_{\mathrm{ff}}=D for the base case, but it can be changed without repercussions as long as the statistical complexity guarantees given in Appendix E.1 are adapted accordingly. We consider the ReLU\operatorname{ReLU} activation function.

Feed-forward.

Define FFNℓ:𝔽D→𝔽D\operatorname{FFN}_{\ell}:\mathbb{F}^{D}\to\mathbb{F}^{D}, applied independently at every one of the nn positions, as

FFNℓ⁡(x):=ΘℓF2​ReLU⁡(ΘℓF1​x+bℓF1)+bℓF2,ReLU⁡(t)=max⁡(0,t),\operatorname{FFN}_{\ell}(x):=\Theta^{F_{2}}_{\ell}\operatorname{ReLU}(\Theta^{F_{1}}_{\ell}x+b^{F_{1}}_{\ell})+b^{F_{2}}_{\ell},\qquad\operatorname{ReLU}(t)=\max(0,t),

where ΘℓF1∈𝔽Dff×D\Theta^{F_{1}}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{F}^{D_{\mathrm{ff}}\times D}, ΘℓF2∈𝔽D×Dff\Theta^{F_{2}}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{F}^{D\times D_{\mathrm{ff}}}, and the biases have matching dimensions. The parameters are shared across all positions.

Transformer block.

Transformer blocks are simply the composition of an attention mechanism with a feed-forward, involving residual streams at each intermediate step. Layer norm is omitted; explanations on this architecture choice can be found in Appendix E.5. Consequently, each of the LL transformer block is

Λ(ℓ+12)\displaystyle\Lambda^{(\ell+\frac{1}{2})} =A(ℓ)⁡(Λ(ℓ))+Λ(ℓ),\displaystyle=\operatorname{A}^{(\ell)}(\Lambda^{(\ell)})+\Lambda^{(\ell)}, (15)
Λ(ℓ+1)\displaystyle\Lambda^{(\ell+1)} =FFNℓ⁡(Λ(ℓ+12))+Λ(ℓ+12).\displaystyle=\operatorname{FFN}_{\ell}(\Lambda^{(\ell+\frac{1}{2})})+\Lambda^{(\ell+\frac{1}{2})}. (16)
Output Layer

The output layer is the pointwise map O:𝔽D→𝔽ν\operatorname{O}:\mathbb{F}^{D}\to\mathbb{F}^{\nu} given by

O⁡(x):=Θout​x+bout\operatorname{O}(x):=\Theta^{\mathrm{out}}x+b^{\mathrm{out}}

where Θout∈𝔽ν×D\Theta^{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu\times D} and bout∈𝔽νb^{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu} are the parameters shared across positions. Thus

T(w):,i=O(Λ:,i(L)(w))(1≤i≤n).T(w)_{:,i}=\operatorname{O}\bigl(\Lambda^{(L)}_{:,i}(w)\bigr)\qquad(1\leq i\leq n).
Attention arithmetic assumptions.

For the transformers considered below, we impose the following conventions, motivated by the positive-sum argument of Li and Cotterell (2025, Appendix B.2, Lemma B.5). Attention sums depend only on the multiset of summands, and inserting zeros does not change them. Nonnegative summands have a nonnegative sum, with +∞+\infty absorbing. There is an integer K𝔽≥1K_{\mathbb{F}}\geq 1, independent of input length, such that any such sum containing more than K𝔽K_{\mathbb{F}} copies of a strictly positive finite value is +∞+\infty. We write

r𝔽≔K𝔽+1.r_{\mathbb{F}}\coloneqq K_{\mathbb{F}}+1. (17)

Stabilized exponentials are nonnegative; zero weights contribute zero even for infinite values. An empty prefix or a softmax denominator equal to 00 or +∞+\infty gives the zero head output. All remaining arithmetic cases are resolved deterministically.

Appendix C Logic

In this section, we define the past fragments of the linear temporal logic and of a two-variable first-order logic, introduced by Li and Cotterell (2025). These fragments are expressively equivalent and provide the link between temporal formulas and the partially-ordered structure studied below, that applies to transformers.

Fix a finite nonempty alphabet Σ\Sigma and a word w=w1⋯wn∈Σ∗w=w_{1}\cdots w_{n}\in\Sigma^{*}. The positions 1,…,n1,\ldots,n are the ordinary token positions. We additionally use n+1n+1 as a virtual logical endpoint: it is an unlabelled position after the word, used only to evaluate word-level formulas.

C.1 Past temporal logic

First we introduce LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], the past fragment of the full linear temporal logic LTL​[N,U,S,P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{N},\textbf{U},\textbf{S},\textbf{P}] that provides several operators, such as next, until, and their past-time counterparts since and past. In our situation, the temporality refers to the positions of a given word, earlier positions thought as being in the past of later positions. The fragment LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] uses only the past operator P, read “at some strictly earlier position”. The restriction to the past operator reflects the strict masking of the attention mechanism. We use its pointed formulas to describe tokenwise transformer outputs, and evaluate word-level formulas at the virtual endpoint.

Definition C.1 (Syntax and semantics of LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}]).

The formulas of LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] are generated by

φ::=⊤∣πa​∣¬φ∣​(φ∧φ)∣​𝐏​φ,a∈Σ.\varphi::=\top\mid\pi_{a}\mid\neg\varphi\mid(\varphi\wedge\varphi)\mid\mathbf{P}\varphi,\qquad a\in\Sigma. (18)

For any position 1≤i≤n+11\leq i\leq n+1, where n+1n+1 is the virtual endpoint, satisfaction is defined inductively by

w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models ⊤always,\displaystyle\top\quad\text{always},
w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models πa⇔i≤n​ and ​wi=a,\displaystyle\pi_{a}\iff i\leq n\text{ and }w_{i}=a,
w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models ¬φ⇔w,i⊧̸φ,\displaystyle\neg\varphi\iff w,i\not\models\varphi,
w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models φ∧ψ⇔w,i⊧φ​ and ​w,i⊧ψ,\displaystyle\varphi\wedge\psi\iff w,i\models\varphi\text{ and }w,i\models\psi,
w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models 𝐏​φ⇔∃j<i​ with ​w,j⊧φ.\displaystyle\mathbf{P}\varphi\iff\exists j<i\text{ with }w,j\models\varphi.

Thus 𝐏\mathbf{P} means “at some strictly earlier position”. The connectives ⊥,∨,⇒\bot,\vee,\Rightarrow are Boolean abbreviations. In particular, ¬𝐏​¬φ\neg\mathbf{P}\neg\varphi means that φ\varphi holds at every earlier position, and is vacuously true at position 11.

Definition C.2.

For a logic formula Ψ∈LTL​[P]\Psi\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], set

w⊧Ψ:=w,n+1⊧Ψ,L⁡(Ψ)≔{w∈Σ∗:w⊧Ψ}.w\models\Psi:=w,n+1\models\Psi,\qquad\qquad L(\Psi)\coloneqq\{w\in\Sigma^{*}:w\models\Psi\}. (19)

Every atomic formula πa\pi_{a}, a∈Σa\in\Sigma, is false at the virtual endpoint. In particular, the formula ¬⋁a∈Σπa\neg\bigvee_{a\in\Sigma}\pi_{a} holds precisely at this endpoint. We also have L⁡(¬𝐏⊤)={ϵ}L(\neg\mathbf{P}\top)=\{{\epsilon}\}.

Example 1.

For a,b,c∈Σa,b,c\in\Sigma,

L⁡(𝐏​πa)\displaystyle L(\mathbf{P}\pi_{a}) =Σ∗​a​Σ∗,\displaystyle=\Sigma^{*}a\Sigma^{*},
L⁡(𝐏⁡(πc∧𝐏⁡(πb∧𝐏​πa)))\displaystyle L\bigl(\mathbf{P}(\pi_{c}\wedge\mathbf{P}(\pi_{b}\wedge\mathbf{P}\pi_{a}))\bigr) =Σ∗​a​Σ∗​b​Σ∗​c​Σ∗,\displaystyle=\Sigma^{*}a\Sigma^{*}b\Sigma^{*}c\Sigma^{*},
L⁡(𝐏⁡(πa∧¬𝐏⊤))\displaystyle L\bigl(\mathbf{P}(\pi_{a}\wedge\neg\mathbf{P}\top)\bigr) =a​Σ∗.\displaystyle=a\Sigma^{*}.

The last formula selects an aa with no predecessor, hence checking for first symbol. Note that we nevertheless can’t express the language Σ∗​a\Sigma^{*}a in LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}].

Lemma C.1 (Prefix invariance).

For u,v∈Σ∗u,v\in\Sigma^{*}, 1≤i≤|u|1\leq i\leq|u|, and φ∈LTL​[P]\varphi\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}],

u,i⊧φ⟺uv,i⊧φ.u,i\models\varphi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad uv,i\models\varphi.
Proof.

Induct on φ\varphi. Atomic predicates depend only on the current symbol, and 𝐏\mathbf{P} quantifies only over positions strictly before ii. ∎

C.2 Past two-variable first-order logic

The second logic that we introduce, a first-order logic, is equivalent to LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}]. The two-variable fragment 𝐅𝐎2​[<]\mathbf{FO}^{2}[<] uses only the position variables x,yx,y, which may be reused under quantifiers. We then further restrict to its past fragment PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<]: each new occurrence of a free variable must be upper bounded by the other, again reflecting strict causal masking. We first give its pointed formulas, then its sentences. Naming two positions with the variables xx and yy is in particular useful for describing an attention query and a key.

The syntax mirrors the construction of LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}]: formulas are built from atomic statements using Boolean connectives and one restricted way of looking into the past.

Definition C.3 (Syntax and semantics of PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<]).

For a∈Σa\in\Sigma and variables x,yx,y, formulas are generated by

θ::=⊤∣πa(x)∣¬θ∣(θ∧θ)∣∃y<x:θ(x,y),\theta::=\top\mid\pi_{a}(x)\mid\neg\theta\mid(\theta\wedge\theta)\mid\exists y<x:\theta(x,y),

where θ⁡(x,y)\theta(x,y) is always defined by a boolean combination of two unary formulas; e.g. θ⁡(x,y)≔ψ⁡(x)∧ψ⁡(y)\theta(x,y)\coloneqq\psi(x)\wedge\psi(y). As in Appendix C.1, positions range over 1,…,n+11,\ldots,n+1, with n+1n+1 the virtual endpoint. For a current position ii and, when needed, an earlier position jj, satisfaction is defined inductively by

w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models ⊤\displaystyle\ \top always,\displaystyle\text{always},
w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models πa​(x)\displaystyle\ \pi_{a}(x) ⟺i≤n​ and ​wi=a,\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\ i\leq n\text{ and }w_{i}=a,
w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models ¬θ\displaystyle\ \neg\theta ⟺w,i⊧̸θ,\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\ w,i\not\models\theta,
w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models θ∧ψ\displaystyle\ \theta\wedge\psi ⟺w,i⊧θ​ and ​w,i⊧ψ,\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\ w,i\models\theta\text{ and }w,i\models\psi,
w,i⊧\displaystyle w,i\models ∃y<x:θ⁡(x,y)\displaystyle\ \exists y<x:\theta(x,y) ⟺∃j<i:w,i,j⊧θ⁡(x,y).\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\ \exists j<i:\ w,i,j\models\theta(x,y).

A formula with one free variable is a pointed formula; a formula with no free variables is a sentence. We use an unbounded existential quantifier only to close a pointed formula into a sentence, as in ∃x:θ⁡(x)\exists x:\theta(x). Boolean connectives and bounded universal quantifiers are abbreviations as usual.

Example 2.

The sentence

∃x:(πc(x)∧∃y<x:(πb(y)∧∃x<y:πa(x)))\exists x:\bigl(\pi_{c}(x)\wedge\exists y<x:\bigl(\pi_{b}(y)\wedge\exists x<y:\pi_{a}(x)\bigr)\bigr)

defines Σ∗​a​Σ∗​b​Σ∗​c​Σ∗\Sigma^{*}a\Sigma^{*}b\Sigma^{*}c\Sigma^{*}. The innermost quantifier reuses xx for the aa-position: within its scope, the outer cc-position is no longer named. This is the first-order analogue of 𝐏⁡(πc∧𝐏⁡(πb∧𝐏​πa))\mathbf{P}(\pi_{c}\wedge\mathbf{P}(\pi_{b}\wedge\mathbf{P}\pi_{a})) in LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}].

Remark C.1.

For every fixed k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and every one-variable formula θ⁡(z)\theta(z), we can express that at least, or exactly, kk earlier positions satisfy θ\theta. Define recursively

∃≥0y<x:θ⁡(y)\displaystyle\exists^{\geq 0}y<x:\theta(y) ≔⁣⊤,\displaystyle\coloneqq\top,
∃≥k+1y<x:θ⁡(y)\displaystyle\exists^{\geq k+1}y<x:\theta(y) ≔∃y<x:(θ(y)∧∃≥kx<y:θ(x)),\displaystyle\coloneqq\exists y<x:\bigl(\theta(y)\wedge\exists^{\geq k}x<y:\theta(x)\bigr),
∃=ky<x:θ⁡(y)\displaystyle\exists^{=k}y<x:\theta(y) ≔(∃≥ky<x:θ⁡(y))∧¬(∃≥k+1y<x:θ⁡(y)).\displaystyle\coloneqq\bigl(\exists^{\geq k}y<x:\theta(y)\bigr)\wedge\neg\bigl(\exists^{\geq k+1}y<x:\theta(y)\bigr).

The recursive definition reuses xx and yy at each level, so it remains in PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<]. These are finite formulas for each fixed threshold kk; they do not add an unbounded counting operation to the logic.

Lemma C.2 (Temporal–first-order correspondence).

The logics LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] and PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] have the same expressive power (Li and Cotterell, 2025, Theorem 2.1). More precisely, every LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] formula is equivalent at each position to a PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] formula with one free variable, and every such PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] formula has an equivalent LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] formula; consequently, their sentences define the same class of languages. Under this correspondence, the basic one-position past test, where φ\varphi has only yy free, is translated as

𝐏φ⟷∃y<x:φ(y).\mathbf{P}\varphi\qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad\exists y<x:\varphi(y).

C.3 Transformers as logic formulas

Under the attention arithmetic assumptions of Appendix B.2, fixed precision lets us describe every coordinate at every ordinary token position by a pointed PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] formula. This is the tokenwise version of the compilation of Li and Cotterell (2025); in particular, it does not use an 𝙴𝙾𝚂\mathtt{EOS} token.

Proposition C.1 (Transformer-to-logic).

Let T∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(L,D,H)T\in\mathcal{FPT}(L,D,H) have output dimension ν\nu. For every output coordinate 1≤d≤ν1\leq d\leq\nu and f∈𝔽f\in\mathbb{F}, there is a pointed formula Φd,fT​(x)∈PFO2​[<]\Phi^{T}_{d,f}(x)\in\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] such that, for every w∈Σ∗w\in\Sigma^{*} and every ordinary position 1≤i≤|w|1\leq i\leq|w|,

w,i⊧Φd,fT(x)⟺T(w)d,i=f.w,i\models\Phi^{T}_{d,f}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T(w)_{d,i}=f. (20)

More generally, the same statement holds for every coordinate and value of each residual layer Λ(ℓ)\Lambda^{(\ell)}.

Construction.

For every layer ℓ\ell, coordinate dd, and f∈𝔽f\in\mathbb{F}, construct Φd,f(ℓ)​(x)\Phi^{(\ell)}_{d,f}(x) so that

w,i⊧Φd,f(ℓ)(x)⟺Λd,i(ℓ)(w)=f.w,i\models\Phi^{(\ell)}_{d,f}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Lambda^{(\ell)}_{d,i}(w)=f. (21)

The embedding case is immediate:

Φd,f(0)​(x)=⋁a∈Σe​(a)d=fπa​(x).\Phi^{(0)}_{d,f}(x)=\bigvee_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in\Sigma\\ e(a)_{d}=f\end{subarray}}\pi_{a}(x). (22)

Every pointwise map G:𝔽m→𝔽rG:\mathbb{F}^{m}\to\mathbb{F}^{r} is a finite lookup table. If its input coordinates are described by φj,g​(x)\varphi_{j,g}(x), its dd-th output has value ff precisely when

Φd,fG​(x)≔⋁𝐠∈𝔽mG​(𝐠)d=f⋀j=1mφj,gj​(x).\Phi^{G}_{d,f}(x)\coloneqq\bigvee_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{F}^{m}\\ G(\mathbf{g})_{d}=f\end{subarray}}\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}\varphi_{j,g_{j}}(x). (23)

Thus projections, residual connections, feed-forward maps, and the final output map preserve the construction using Boolean operations only.

It remains to consider one attention head. Its query, key, and value vectors are pointwise maps, so the preceding display gives formulas for every 𝐪,𝐤,𝐯∈𝔽Dh\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{F}^{D_{h}}. Denote the corresponding formulas by

Q𝐪(ℓ,h)​(x),K𝐤(ℓ,h)​(y),V𝐯(ℓ,h)​(y);\mathrm{Q}^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{q}}(x),\qquad\mathrm{K}^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{k}}(y),\qquad\mathrm{V}^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{v}}(y);

for example, w,i⊧Q𝐪(ℓ,h)​(x)w,i\models\mathrm{Q}^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{q}}(x) if and only if Q:,i=𝐪Q_{:,i}=\mathbf{q}. The relevant query–key/value relation is the two-variable formula

θ𝐪,𝐤,𝐯​(x,y)≡Q𝐪(ℓ,h)​(x)∧K𝐤(ℓ,h)​(y)∧V𝐯(ℓ,h)​(y).\theta_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{v}}(x,y)\quad\equiv\quad\mathrm{Q}^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{q}}(x)\wedge\mathrm{K}^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{k}}(y)\wedge\mathrm{V}^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{v}}(y). (24)

For each current query position xx, the maximum score, softmax denominator, and weighted value sum are finite case distinctions over the multiplicities of earlier positions yy satisfying these relations. In particular, the required fixed thresholds vary with the query position and are expressed directly in PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] by

∃≥ry<x:θ𝐪,𝐤,𝐯​(x,y),\exists^{\geq r}y<x:\theta_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{k},\mathbf{v}}(x,y), (25)

and their exact-count Boolean combinations, as in Remark C.1. Let Ξ𝐪,d,f(ℓ,h)​(x)\Xi^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{q},d,f}(x) denote the resulting finite Boolean combination that selects the cases in which head hh outputs value ff in coordinate dd for query 𝐪\mathbf{q}. Its output formula is

Φd,fA,(ℓ,h)​(x)=⋁𝐪∈𝔽Dh(Q𝐪(ℓ,h)​(x)∧Ξ𝐪,d,f(ℓ,h)​(x)).\Phi^{\operatorname{A},(\ell,h)}_{d,f}(x)=\bigvee_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{F}^{D_{h}}}\left(\mathrm{Q}^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{q}}(x)\wedge\Xi^{(\ell,h)}_{\mathbf{q},d,f}(x)\right). (26)

Fixed precision gives finitely many query cases, and the arithmetic assumptions of Appendix B.2 let us clip multiplicities at r𝔽r_{\mathbb{F}}. Thus only finitely many cases are needed.

Consequently, attention produces formulas satisfying equation 21 for the next sublayer, and the pointwise steps complete the induction over ℓ\ell. Applying the final output lookup formula equation 23 yields equation 20. ∎

All formulas in Proposition C.1 are evaluated at ordinary token positions. By Lemma C.2, each has an equivalent pointed LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] formula, using the PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] presentation to keep the current position xx and the earlier position yy explicit.

C.4 Partially ordered automata

Word-level formulas define languages, whereas the pointed formulas equation 20 describe an output at each token. The corresponding automata verifying the formulas are respectively DFAs and Mealy machines.

Definition C.4 (Deterministic Finite Automaton).

A DFA is a tuple 𝒜=(Q,Σ,δ,q0,FA)\mathcal{A}=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_{0},F_{A}), with finite state set QQ, initial state q0q_{0}, accepting set FA⊆QF_{A}\subseteq Q, and transition function δ:Q×Σ→Q\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q. By abuse of notation, extend δ\delta to words by iterating over their letters:

δ⁡(q,ϵ)=q,δ⁡(q,u​a)=δ⁡(δ⁡(q,u),a).\delta(q,{\epsilon})=q,\qquad\delta(q,ua)=\delta(\delta(q,u),a).

It recognises the language L⁡(𝒜)={u:δ⁡(q0,u)∈FA}L(\mathcal{A})=\{u:\delta(q_{0},u)\in F_{A}\}.

For our results, we do not need the following Mealy machine construction, as we work with the difference function which is expressed by a poDFA. Nevertheless, Mealy machines describe individual transformers: they process the input left to right and emit an output vector at every position. We shall see also that the height arguments can directly apply on Mealy machines. In general, Mealy machines provide the opportunity to deepen the ordered-automaton analyses of the transformers outside of the student–teacher learning framework.

Definition C.5 (Mealy Machine).

A Mealy machine ℳ=(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0,λ)\mathcal{M}=(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_{0},\lambda) is an automaton in the same way as the DFA C.4, but has a finite output alphabet Γ\Gamma, an output map λ:Q×Σ→Γ\lambda:Q\times\Sigma\to\Gamma and no notion of accepting states. On input w=w1⋯wnw=w_{1}\cdots w_{n}, it emits

ℳ(w)i=λ(δ(q0,w1:i−1),wi)(1≤i≤n).\mathcal{M}(w)_{i}=\lambda(\delta(q_{0},w_{1:i-1}),w_{i})\qquad(1\leq i\leq n).

Intuitively, Mealy machines are automata such that their restricted behaviour, with respect to one output symbol, resembles a DFA.

Definition C.6 (Partially ordered automata).

A DFA 𝒜\mathcal{A} or a Mealy machine ℳ\mathcal{M}, is said to be partially ordered if reachability of its states is antisymmetric, equivalently if it contains no cycles but self-loops. Its height is the largest number of strict state changes along a run:

ht(ℳ)=maxw∈Σ∗|{i:δ(q0,w1:i)≠δ(q0,w1:i−1)}|,\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{M})=\max_{w\in\Sigma^{*}}\bigl|\{i:\delta(q_{0},w_{1:i})\neq\delta(q_{0},w_{1:i-1})\}\bigr|,

with the same definition for 𝒜\mathcal{A}. It is reduced if all states are reachable and if two distinct states have different future behaviour.

Remark.

Different future behaviours for DFAs means that for any two distinct states representers w,w′w,w^{\prime}, there exists a suffix v∈Σ∗v\in\Sigma^{*} such that, w.l.o.g. δ⁡(w,v)∈FA\delta(w,v)\in F_{A} while δ⁡(w′,v)∉FA\delta(w^{\prime},v)\notin F_{A}. For Mealy machines, it similarly means that for some suffix concatenation, the future emitted sequences must disagree.

We recall the language-level correspondence established by Li and Cotterell (2025, Section 4 and Appendix C).

Proposition C.2.

For every Ψ∈LTL​[P]\Psi\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], the language L(Ψ)={w:w,|w|+1⊧Ψ}L(\Psi)=\{w:w,|w|+1\models\Psi\} is regular and its reduced DFA is partially ordered. The same holds for the equivalent word-level PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] formulas.

Proof.

Li and Cotterell show that the syntactic monoid of an LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}]-definable language is ℛ\mathcal{R}-trivial (Li and Cotterell, 2025, Appendix C): distinct monoid elements have distinct principal right ideals. The characterisation of Brzozowski (1980) identifies these regular languages exactly with those whose reduced DFA is partially ordered. The PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] statement follows from Lemma C.2. ∎

The states of this automaton have the usual right-context interpretation given by Myhill–Nerode (Myhill, 1957; Nerode, 1958).

Proposition C.3.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the reduced DFA of a regular language ℒ\mathcal{L}. For any u,v∈Σ∗u,v\in\Sigma^{*},

δ(q0,u)=δ(q0,v)⟺∀z∈Σ∗:(uz∈ℒ⟺vz∈ℒ).\delta(q_{0},u)=\delta(q_{0},v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall z\in\Sigma^{*}:\quad(uz\in\mathcal{L}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ vz\in\mathcal{L}).

Thus its states are precisely the classes of prefixes with the same accepting continuations. For ℒ=L⁡(Ψ)\mathcal{L}=L(\Psi), these classes form the states of the reduced poDFA above.

Proof.

Prefixes reaching the same state have the same acceptance decision on every continuation, by determinism. Conversely, two distinct states of a reduced DFA admit a distinguishing continuation. Every state is reachable, so this identifies the states with the right-context classes. ∎

We now apply this correspondence to the tokenwise transformer formulas 20. Their past tests are recognised by poDFAs, and the current letter determines the output together with the states of these automata.

Proposition C.4 (Transformers as partially-ordered Mealy machines).

Every transformer admitting the formulas equation 20 is realised by a finite partially ordered Mealy machine with output alphabet Γ=𝔽ν\Gamma=\mathbb{F}^{\nu}:

ℳT(w)i=T(w):,i(1≤i≤|w|).\mathcal{M}_{T}(w)_{i}=T(w)_{:,i}\qquad(1\leq i\leq|w|).

In particular, Proposition C.1 provides these formulas for the transformers of Appendix B.2.

Proof.

Translate the pointed PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] formulas into equivalent LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] formulas Ψd,fT\Psi^{T}_{d,f} by Lemma C.2, and let 𝒫\mathcal{P} collect their distinct past subformulas χ=𝐏​ψ\chi=\mathbf{P}\psi. For each χ\chi, Proposition C.2 provides a reduced poDFA 𝒜χ=(Qχ,Σ,δχ,q0,χ,Fχ)\mathcal{A}_{\chi}=(Q_{\chi},\Sigma,\delta_{\chi},q_{0,\chi},F_{\chi}) recognising L⁡(χ)L(\chi). After a prefix uu, its acceptance bit gives exactly the corresponding past test at the next token:

δχ(q0,χ,u)∈Fχ⟺uσ,|u|+1⊧χ(σ∈Σ).\delta_{\chi}(q_{0,\chi},u)\in F_{\chi}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\sigma,|u|+1\models\chi\qquad(\sigma\in\Sigma).

Indeed, both sides ask whether ψ\psi holds at some position in uu; prefix invariance preserves those truth values.

Take the reachable part of the product of these poDFAs, with

q0=(q0,χ)χ∈𝒫,δ⁡(q,σ)=(δχ​(qχ,σ))χ∈𝒫.q_{0}=(q_{0,\chi})_{\chi\in\mathcal{P}},\qquad\delta(q,\sigma)=\bigl(\delta_{\chi}(q_{\chi},\sigma)\bigr)_{\chi\in\mathcal{P}}.

For each current letter σ\sigma, evaluate Ψd,fT\Psi^{T}_{d,f} by replacing πa\pi_{a} with 𝟏{σ=a}\mathbf{1}\{\sigma=a\} and each past test χ\chi with 𝟏{qχ∈Fχ}\mathbf{1}\{q_{\chi}\in F_{\chi}\}, respecting Boolean connectives. Set λ​(q,σ)d\lambda(q,\sigma)_{d} to the unique ff for which this evaluation is true. Equation equation 20 ensures existence and uniqueness on reachable states. The output uses the state before reading σ\sigma, so the past remains strict. Finally, every component can only advance in its reachability order; their finite product is therefore partially ordered. If 𝒫\mathcal{P} is empty, the product has one state. ∎

This proposition establishes the inherent ordered structure of the transformers, using Mealy machines. We shall see quickly that the difference function between two transformers translates naturally in the other ordered automaton that we defined earlier: the poDFA.

Remark C.2.

Each Φd,fT​(x)\Phi^{T}_{d,f}(x) gives a Boolean output on transitions of this machine. Testing it at the last ordinary token need not define a poDFA language: πa​(x)\pi_{a}(x) would give Σ∗​a\Sigma^{*}a, whose reduced DFA has a nontrivial cycle when |Σ|≥2|\Sigma|\geq 2. The poDFAs used above instead recognise past tests at the virtual endpoint. Importantly, a fixed Mealy state may still emit different vectors on different input letters.

To identify the states intrinsically, write

Tu(z)≔(T(uz):,|u|+j)j=1|z|.T_{u}(z)\coloneqq\bigl(T(uz)_{:,|u|+j}\bigr)_{j=1}^{|z|}.

This is the sequence emitted on the continuation zz after reading uu; it excludes the outputs already emitted on uu.

Proposition C.5.

For a transformer satisfying Proposition C.4, there is a unique reduced Mealy machine, up to isomorphism. Its states are the classes of

u∼Tv⟺∀z∈Σ∗:Tu(z)=Tv(z),u\sim_{T}v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall z\in\Sigma^{*}:\ T_{u}(z)=T_{v}(z),

and its transitions and outputs are

q0=[ϵ],δ([u],a)=[ua],λ([u],a)=T(ua):,|u|+1.q_{0}=[{\epsilon}],\qquad\delta([u],a)=[ua],\qquad\lambda([u],a)=T(ua)_{:,|u|+1}.

This reduced machine is partially ordered. Consequently,

δ(q0,u)=δ(q0,v)⟺∀z∈Σ∗:Tu(z)=Tv(z).\delta(q_{0},u)=\delta(q_{0},v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall z\in\Sigma^{*}:\ T_{u}(z)=T_{v}(z).
Proof.

Causality gives Tu​(a​z)=Tu​(a)​Tu​a​(z)T_{u}(az)=T_{u}(a)\,T_{ua}(z), with concatenation of output sequences. Hence u∼Tvu\sim_{T}v implies equal outputs on aa and ua∼Tvaua\sim_{T}va, so the displayed maps are well defined. Equal states of the finite machine in Proposition C.4 imply equivalent prefixes; our construction is therefore a finite quotient. All classes are reachable and distinct classes have a distinguishing continuation. In any reduced realisation, these same classes correspond bijectively to states, proving reducedness and uniqueness.

Finally, reduction preserves partial order: repeatedly traversing a nontrivial quotient cycle would force infinitely many state changes in the original finite partially ordered machine, a contradiction. ∎

C.5 Past subformulas and automaton height

We relate past subformulas to the height of their associated automata. Word satisfaction is always evaluated at the virtual endpoint |w|+1|w|+1 of Appendix C.1.

Definition C.7 (Subformulas).

For Ψ∈LTL​[P]\Psi\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], let Sub⁡(Ψ)\operatorname{Sub}(\Psi) be the set of its syntactically distinct subformulas, including Ψ\Psi itself. Recursively,

Sub⁡(⊤)\displaystyle\operatorname{Sub}(\top) ={⊤},\displaystyle=\{\top\}, Sub⁡(πa)\displaystyle\operatorname{Sub}(\pi_{a}) ={πa},\displaystyle=\{\pi_{a}\},
Sub⁡(¬φ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Sub}(\neg\varphi) ={¬φ}∪Sub⁡(φ),\displaystyle=\{\neg\varphi\}\cup\operatorname{Sub}(\varphi), Sub⁡(𝐏​φ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Sub}(\mathbf{P}\varphi) ={𝐏​φ}∪Sub⁡(φ),\displaystyle=\{\mathbf{P}\varphi\}\cup\operatorname{Sub}(\varphi),
Sub⁡(φ∧ψ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Sub}(\varphi\wedge\psi) ={φ∧ψ}∪Sub⁡(φ)∪Sub⁡(ψ).\displaystyle=\{\varphi\wedge\psi\}\cup\operatorname{Sub}(\varphi)\cup\operatorname{Sub}(\psi).

The past subformulas are those whose outermost operator is 𝐏\mathbf{P}: Sub𝐏⁡(Ψ)≔{𝐏​φ:𝐏​φ∈Sub⁡(Ψ)}\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi)\coloneqq\{\mathbf{P}\varphi:\mathbf{P}\varphi\in\operatorname{Sub}(\Psi)\}.

Definition C.8 (Past profile).

For any formula Ψ∈LTL​[P]\Psi\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], we define the past profile of a word u∈Σ∗u\in\Sigma^{*} as the vector

profΨ(u)∈{0,1}Sub𝐏⁡(Ψ),profΨ(u)(𝐏φ)=𝟏{u,|u|+1⊧𝐏φ}.\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u)\in\{0,1\}^{\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi)},\qquad\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u)(\mathbf{P}\varphi)=\mathbf{1}\{u,|u|+1\models\mathbf{P}\varphi\}. (27)

It records which past subformulas hold after reading uu, at its virtual endpoint |u|+1|u|+1.

Example 3.

For Ψ=𝐏⁡(πb∧𝐏​πa)\Psi=\mathbf{P}(\pi_{b}\wedge\mathbf{P}\pi_{a}), order the profile coordinates as (𝐏​πa,Ψ)(\mathbf{P}\pi_{a},\Psi). For distinct a,ba,b, the profiles of ϵ,a,a​b{\epsilon},a,ab are respectively (0,0),(1,0),(1,1)(0,0),(1,0),(1,1).

For a language L⊆Σ∗L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}, we note the left residual at a prefix uu with respect to a language LL as

u−1​L≔{v∈Σ∗:u​v∈L}.u^{-1}L\coloneqq\{v\in\Sigma^{*}:uv\in L\}.
Lemma C.3.

Let u1,u2∈Σ∗u_{1},u_{2}\in\Sigma^{*}. If

profΨ⁡(u1)=profΨ⁡(u2),\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u_{1})=\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u_{2}),

then,

u1−1​L​(Ψ)=u2−1​L​(Ψ);u_{1}^{-1}L(\Psi)=u_{2}^{-1}L(\Psi);

equivalently for every v∈Σ∗v\in\Sigma^{*},

u1v∈L(Ψ)⟺u2v∈L(Ψ).u_{1}v\in L(\Psi)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_{2}v\in L(\Psi).
Proof.

Write li=|ui|l_{i}=|u_{i}| and m=|v|m=|v|. By structural induction on φ∈Sub⁡(Ψ)\varphi\in\operatorname{Sub}(\Psi), we show that, for 0≤k≤m0\leq k\leq m,

u1v,l1+k+1⊧φ⟺u2v,l2+k+1⊧φ.u_{1}v,l_{1}+k+1\models\varphi\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_{2}v,l_{2}+k+1\models\varphi. (28)

First, the atomic case compares the same suffix symbol, or the two virtual endpoints; hence the equivalence holds. The Boolean cases follow immediately.

Now consider φ=𝐏​θ\varphi=\mathbf{P}\theta. For i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\},

ui​v,li+k+1⊧𝐏​θ⇔profΨ⁡(ui)​(𝐏​θ)=1∨∃ 0≤j<k:ui​v,li+j+1⊧θ.u_{i}v,l_{i}+k+1\models\mathbf{P}\theta\iff\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u_{i})(\mathbf{P}\theta)=1\ \lor\ \exists\ 0\leq j<k:\ u_{i}v,l_{i}+j+1\models\theta.

The first case says that θ\theta already has a witness in uiu_{i}, which is stored in the profile. The second says that it has a witness in the first kk positions of vv. By (PR), the first cases agree; by the induction hypothesis, so do the second. Thus the equivalence holds. Taking φ=Ψ\varphi=\Psi and k=mk=m proves the claim. ∎

Corollary C.1.

Let Ψ∈LTL​[P]\Psi\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] and let AΨA_{\Psi} be its minimal DFA. If two prefixes u1,u2∈Σ∗u_{1},u_{2}\in\Sigma^{*} have the same past profile, then they reach the same state of AΨA_{\Psi}.

Proof.

Lemma C.3 gives us that for every suffix v∈Σ∗v\in\Sigma^{*},

u1v∈L(Ψ)⟺u2v∈L(Ψ).u_{1}v\in L(\Psi)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_{2}v\in L(\Psi).

This is precisely the characterisation of Proposition C.3. ∎

Definition C.9.

For b,b′∈{0,1}Sub𝐏⁡(Ψ)b,b^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi)}, write b⪯b′b\preceq b^{\prime} when

∀χ∈Sub𝐏⁡(Ψ),b⁡(χ)≤b′​(χ).\forall\chi\in\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi),\qquad b(\chi)\leq b^{\prime}(\chi).

Write b≺b′b\prec b^{\prime} when b⪯b′b\preceq b^{\prime} and b≠b′b\neq b^{\prime}.

Lemma C.4.

For all u,v∈Σ∗u,v\in\Sigma^{*},

profΨ⁡(u)⪯profΨ⁡(u​v).\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u)\preceq\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(uv).
Proof.

Let 𝐏​θ∈Sub𝐏⁡(Ψ)\mathbf{P}\theta\in\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi) and suppose that profΨ⁡(u)​(𝐏​θ)=1\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u)(\mathbf{P}\theta)=1. By definition, there is a position m<|u|+1m<|u|+1 such that u,m⊧θu,m\models\theta. By Lemma C.1, u​v,m⊧θuv,m\models\theta; also m<|u​v|+1m<|uv|+1. Hence u​v,|u​v|+1⊧𝐏​θuv,|uv|+1\models\mathbf{P}\theta, so profΨ⁡(u​v)​(𝐏​θ)=1\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(uv)(\mathbf{P}\theta)=1. This holds for every coordinate. ∎

Lemma C.5.

Let SS be a finite set and let

b0≺b1≺⋯≺brin ​{0,1}Sb_{0}\prec b_{1}\prec\cdots\prec b_{r}\qquad\text{in }\{0,1\}^{S}

under the coordinate-wise order. Then r≤|S|r\leq|S|.

Proof.

For every ii, let Si⊆SS_{i}\subseteq S be the support of bib_{i}, namely the set of coordinates on which bib_{i} is 11. The strict inequalities give

S0⊊S1⊊⋯⊊Sr⊆S.S_{0}\subsetneq S_{1}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq S_{r}\subseteq S.

Every strict inclusion increases cardinality by at least one. Thus there are at most |S||S| strict inclusions, proving r≤|S|r\leq|S|. ∎

Lemma C.6.
