Let u0,…,ur∈Σ∗u_{0},\ldots,u_{r}\in\Sigma^{*} be a sequence of prefixes such that, for every 0≤i<r0\leq i<r, there is a word xi∈Σ∗x_{i}\in\Sigma^{*} satisfying

ui+1=ui​xiandui−1​L​(Ψ)≠ui+1−1​L​(Ψ).u_{i+1}=u_{i}x_{i}\qquad\text{and}\qquad u_{i}^{-1}L(\Psi)\neq u_{i+1}^{-1}L(\Psi).

Then

r≤|Sub𝐏⁡(Ψ)|.r\leq\bigl|\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi)\bigr|.
Proof.

By Lemma C.4,

profΨ⁡(ui)⪯profΨ⁡(ui+1)(0≤i<r).\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u_{i})\preceq\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}(u_{i+1})\qquad(0\leq i<r).

If two consecutive profiles were equal, Lemma C.3 would imply ui−1​L​(Ψ)=ui+1−1​L​(Ψ)u_{i}^{-1}L(\Psi)=u_{i+1}^{-1}L(\Psi), contrary to assumption. Hence each displayed relation is strict. Lemma C.5, applied with S=Sub𝐏⁡(Ψ)S=\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi), gives the result. ∎

We finally combine the previous definitions and results for the following result. In particular, the bound C0C_{0} from Eq. 2 is an application of this theorem:

Theorem C.1 (Past subformulas bound automaton height).

For Ψ∈LTL​[P]\Psi\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], the reduced DFA 𝒜Ψ\mathcal{A}_{\Psi} of L⁡(Ψ)L(\Psi) satisfies

ht⁡(𝒜Ψ)≤|Sub𝐏⁡(Ψ)|.\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}_{\Psi})\leq|\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi)|.
Proof.

The bound follows from Lemma C.6. ∎

We can directly convey the above result to the Mealy machine. Intuitively, our transformers from Appendix B.2 are the Mealy machines made of the pointed formulas given in 20.

Corollary C.2.

For a finite family 𝒢\mathcal{G} of pointed LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] formulas, the reduced Mealy machine ℳ𝒢\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{G}} emitting their truth values at each token similarly satisfies

ht⁡(ℳ𝒢)≤|⋃φ∈𝒢Sub𝐏⁡(φ)|.\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{G}})\leq\left|\bigcup_{\varphi\in\mathcal{G}}\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\varphi)\right|.
Proof.

For the Mealy bound, store the shared past profile over ⋃φ∈𝒢Sub𝐏⁡(φ)\bigcup_{\varphi\in\mathcal{G}}\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\varphi). Together with the next letter, it determines the current truth values and the updated profile: the bit for 𝐏​θ\mathbf{P}\theta becomes its old value OR the current truth of θ\theta. Thus these profiles form a Mealy realisation. Each bit changes at most once, giving the stated height; reduction cannot increase it. ∎

Appendix D Length Generalization

For two ℱ​𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{FPT}s given by Ts,TtT_{s},T_{t} sharing Σ\Sigma, 𝔽\mathbb{F}, and output dimension ν\nu, the difference function from Section 3.1 is

Δ(w)≔𝟏{∃ 1≤i≤|w|:Ts(w):,i≠Tt(w):,i}.\Delta(w)\coloneqq\mathbf{1}\{\exists\,1\leq i\leq|w|:\ T_{s}(w)_{:,i}\neq T_{t}(w)_{:,i}\}. (29)

We give two height bounds for its reduced poDFA 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta}. We use the arithmetic assumptions of Appendix B.2, with p=|𝔽|p=|\mathbb{F}| and r𝔽=K𝔽+1r_{\mathbb{F}}=K_{\mathbb{F}}+1.

D.1 Bounding the height with past subformulas

We count the past subformulas needed to describe one transformer’s outputs, then combine the two families into a formula for the difference function.

Lemma D.1 (Simultaneous output representation).

Under these arithmetic hypotheses, let T∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(L,D,H)T\in\mathcal{FPT}(L,D,H) have output dimension ν\nu, and put Dh=D/HD_{h}=D/H. There are formulas Φd,fT∈LTL​[P]\Phi^{T}_{d,f}\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}], for 1≤d≤ν1\leq d\leq\nu and f∈𝔽f\in\mathbb{F}, such that, for every w∈Σ∗w\in\Sigma^{*} and 1≤i≤|w|1\leq i\leq|w|,

w,i⊧Φd,fT⟺T(w)d,i=f.w,i\models\Phi^{T}_{d,f}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T(w)_{d,i}=f.

Their shared collection of distinct past subformulas satisfies

𝒫⁡(T)≔⋃d=1ν⋃f∈𝔽Sub𝐏⁡(Φd,fT),|𝒫⁡(T)|≤B⁡(T)≔r𝔽​L​D​pD/H+1.\mathcal{P}(T)\coloneqq\bigcup_{d=1}^{\nu}\ \bigcup_{f\in\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Phi^{T}_{d,f}),\qquad|\mathcal{P}(T)|\leq B(T)\coloneqq r_{\mathbb{F}}LD\,p^{D/H+1}. (30)
Proof.

Follow the layerwise construction of Appendix C.3, now directly in LTL​[P]\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}]. At layer 00, the embedding coordinates are described by

Φ(0)d,f=⋁a:e​(a)d=fπa.\Phi^{(0)}_{d,f}=\bigvee_{a\,:\,e(a)_{d}=f}\pi_{a}.

Moreover, if a pointwise map gg sends input coordinates with values (f1,…,fr)(f_{1},\ldots,f_{r}) to g⁡(f1,…,fr)g(f_{1},\ldots,f_{r}), then its output value ff is described by the Boolean combination

⋁(f1,…,fr):g⁡(f1,…,fr)=f⋀j=1rΦj,fj.\bigvee_{(f_{1},\ldots,f_{r})\,:\,g(f_{1},\ldots,f_{r})=f}\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{r}\Phi_{j,f_{j}}.

Thus projections, feed-forward maps, residuals, and the output map add no past operators. Only attention does.

Fix a layer ℓ\ell and a head hh, suppressing these indices below. For each key vector 𝐤∈𝔽Dh\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{F}^{D_{h}}, coordinate d≤Dhd\leq D_{h}, and value f∈𝔽f\in\mathbb{F}, let θ𝐤,d,f\theta_{\mathbf{k},d,f} describe the unary condition K:,i=𝐤K_{:,i}=\mathbf{k} and Vd,i=fV_{d,i}=f. These pointwise predicates add no past operators. Writing θ⁡(y)\theta(y) for their unary PFO2​[<]\textbf{PFO}^{2}[<] form, we describe the clipped counts

c𝐤,d,f(i)=min{r𝔽,|{j<i:K:,j=𝐤,Vd,j=f}|}c_{\mathbf{k},d,f}(i)=\min\!\left\{r_{\mathbb{F}},\bigl|\{j<i:K_{:,j}=\mathbf{k},\ V_{d,j}=f\}\bigr|\right\}

using the threshold tests

∃=ry<x:θ⁡(y)(0≤r<r𝔽),∃≥r𝔽y<x:θ⁡(y).\exists^{=r}y<x:\theta(y)\quad(0\leq r<r_{\mathbb{F}}),\qquad\exists^{\geq r_{\mathbb{F}}}y<x:\theta(y). (31)

By Remark C.1, each successive at-least threshold adds one outer 𝐏\mathbf{P} to the conjunction of θ\theta with the previous threshold. Thresholds 1,…,r𝔽1,\ldots,r_{\mathbb{F}} share their shorter expansions, and exact counts are Boolean combinations of successive thresholds (threshold 00 is ⊤\top). Hence all tests for one θ\theta add at most r𝔽r_{\mathbb{F}} distinct past subformulas.

Fix an output coordinate dd. The current query 𝐪=Q:,i\mathbf{q}=Q_{:,i} and the clipped-count vector

𝐜i=(c𝐤,d,f​(i))𝐤∈𝔽Dh,d≤Dh,f∈𝔽\mathbf{c}_{i}=\bigl(c_{\mathbf{k},d,f}(i)\bigr)_{\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{F}^{D_{h}},\;d\leq D_{h},\;f\in\mathbb{F}}

determine the head output. Indeed, these data identify the present keys, the maximum score, and each stabilized exponential a𝐤a_{\mathbf{k}}. If some a𝐤=+∞a_{\mathbf{k}}=+\infty, or if

c𝐤,d,f​(i)=r𝔽anda𝐤>0,c_{\mathbf{k},d,f}(i)=r_{\mathbb{F}}\quad\text{and}\quad a_{\mathbf{k}}>0,

then the denominator overflows and the head output is zero. Otherwise, every type with a positive exponential has its exact multiplicity recorded, while zero terms contribute nothing. Multiset summation then determines the denominator, the weights, and the weighted value sum. Hence, for a finite lookup function AdA_{d},

Attd,i=Ad​(𝐪,𝐜i).\operatorname{Att}_{d,i}=A_{d}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{c}_{i}).

Expanding this finite lookup into Boolean cases reuses only the threshold tests above, and so introduces no further past subformulas.

There are

|𝔽Dh|​Dh​|𝔽|=Dh​pDh+1|\mathbb{F}^{D_{h}}|\,D_{h}\,|\mathbb{F}|=D_{h}p^{D_{h}+1}

key–coordinate–value types per head. Thus, if 𝒫ℓ\mathcal{P}_{\ell} denotes the past subformulas available after layer ℓ\ell, then

|𝒫ℓ∖𝒫ℓ−1|≤r𝔽​H​Dh​pDh+1=r𝔽​D​pD/H+1.|\mathcal{P}_{\ell}\setminus\mathcal{P}_{\ell-1}|\leq r_{\mathbb{F}}HD_{h}p^{D_{h}+1}=r_{\mathbb{F}}Dp^{D/H+1}.

Summing this bound over the LL layers proves equation 30. All ν\nu output coordinates and all f∈𝔽f\in\mathbb{F} reuse the same collection, so the final output map adds no factor. ∎

Remark D.1.

We count distinct past subformulas, not occurrences or Boolean formula size. A general ∃y<x:θ⁡(x,y)\exists y<x:\theta(x,y) need not translate into a single 𝐏\mathbf{P}-subformula. Here all counted predicates depend only on yy; the current query is handled outside the past operators by Boolean cases.

The predicates Φd,fT\Phi^{T}_{d,f} describe the outputs of the Mealy machines from Appendix C.4. Comparing these predicates and checking for a mismatch anywhere in the word gives the difference function.

Proposition D.1 (Difference function as a logic formula).

Let Ts,TtT_{s},T_{t} be student and teacher transformers satisfying the preceding hypotheses, over the same alphabet and precision set, with the same output dimension ν\nu. Using the formulas of Lemma D.1, define

ψΔ\displaystyle\psi_{\Delta} ≔⋁d=1ν⋁f∈𝔽(Φd,fTs∧¬Φd,fTt),\displaystyle\coloneqq\bigvee_{d=1}^{\nu}\ \bigvee_{f\in\mathbb{F}}\bigl(\Phi^{T_{s}}_{d,f}\wedge\neg\Phi^{T_{t}}_{d,f}\bigr), (32)
ΨΔ\displaystyle\Psi_{\Delta} ≔𝐏​ψΔ.\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbf{P}\psi_{\Delta}. (33)

Then

w⊧ΨΔ⟺Δ(w)=1,w\models\Psi_{\Delta}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Delta(w)=1,

and

|Sub𝐏⁡(ΨΔ)|≤B⁡(Ts)+B⁡(Tt)+1.|\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi_{\Delta})|\leq B(T_{s})+B(T_{t})+1. (34)

Moreover, L⁡(ΨΔ)​Σ∗=L⁡(ΨΔ)L(\Psi_{\Delta})\Sigma^{*}=L(\Psi_{\Delta}).

Proof.

At each token, ψΔ\psi_{\Delta} holds exactly when an output coordinate differs. Thus 𝐏​ψΔ\mathbf{P}\psi_{\Delta}, evaluated at |w|+1|w|+1, expresses Δ⁡(w)=1\Delta(w)=1 (and is false on ϵ{\epsilon}). Boolean operations add no past subformulas:

Sub𝐏⁡(ΨΔ)⊆𝒫⁡(Ts)∪𝒫⁡(Tt)∪{𝐏​ψΔ}.\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathbf{P}}(\Psi_{\Delta})\subseteq\mathcal{P}(T_{s})\cup\mathcal{P}(T_{t})\cup\{\mathbf{P}\psi_{\Delta}\}.

This proves the count. Causality preserves an existing mismatch under right concatenation, proving persistence. ∎

Corollary D.1.

The reduced DFA 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} of L⁡(ΨΔ)L(\Psi_{\Delta}) is partially ordered and satisfies

ht⁡(𝒜Δ)≤B⁡(Ts)+B⁡(Tt)+1=r𝔽​(Ls​Ds​pDs/Hs+1+Lt​Dt​pDt/Ht+1)+1.\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}_{\Delta})\leq B(T_{s})+B(T_{t})+1=r_{\mathbb{F}}\bigl(L_{s}D_{s}p^{D_{s}/H_{s}+1}+L_{t}D_{t}p^{D_{t}/H_{t}+1}\bigr)+1.

If Δ\Delta is not identically zero, 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} has a unique accepting state, which is absorbing.

Proof.

Apply Proposition C.2 and Theorem C.1 to ΨΔ\Psi_{\Delta}, then use equation 34. Every accepted prefix has residual Σ∗\Sigma^{*} by persistence, so all accepting prefixes reach the same absorbing state by Proposition C.3. ∎

Remark D.2 (Mealy-machine interpretation).

Let ℳT\mathcal{M}_{T} be the reduced Mealy machine of TT. The shared-profile argument of Appendix C.5 gives ht⁡(ℳT)≤B⁡(T)\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{M}_{T})\leq B(T). Running the two machines in parallel until their outputs differ gives

ht⁡(𝒜Δ)≤ht⁡(ℳTs)+ht⁡(ℳTt)+1.\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}_{\Delta})\leq\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{M}_{T_{s}})+\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{M}_{T_{t}})+1. (35)

Each strict product transition advances at least one component; entering the absorbing bad state adds at most one. Reduction cannot increase height.

D.2 Bounding the height with temporal profiles

We bound the same difference-function poDFA 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} using past nesting depth. This removes the exponential dependence on D/HD/H and gives a polynomial bound in depth, of degree s=|Σ|s=|\Sigma|.

Definition D.1 (Past depth and temporal profiles).

The past depth of a formula is defined by

pd⁡(⊤)\displaystyle\operatorname{pd}(\top) =pd⁡(πa)=0,\displaystyle=\operatorname{pd}(\pi_{a})=0, pd⁡(¬φ)\displaystyle\operatorname{pd}(\neg\varphi) =pd⁡(φ),\displaystyle=\operatorname{pd}(\varphi),
pd⁡(𝐏​φ)\displaystyle\operatorname{pd}(\mathbf{P}\varphi) =1+pd⁡(φ),\displaystyle=1+\operatorname{pd}(\varphi), pd⁡(φ∧ψ)\displaystyle\operatorname{pd}(\varphi\wedge\psi) =max⁡{pd⁡(φ),pd⁡(ψ)}.\displaystyle=\max\{\operatorname{pd}(\varphi),\operatorname{pd}(\psi)\}.

For w∈Σ∗w\in\Sigma^{*}, write w<i=w1⋯wi−1w_{<i}=w_{1}\cdots w_{i-1} and define

U0(w)=⋆,Uk+1(w)={(wi,Uk(w<i)):1≤i≤|w|},U_{0}(w)=\star,\qquad U_{k+1}(w)=\bigl\{(w_{i},U_{k}(w_{<i})):1\leq i\leq|w|\bigr\}, (36)

where ⋆\star is a fixed symbol. Unlike profΨ\operatorname{prof}_{\Psi}, the profile UkU_{k} does not depend on a particular formula: it records which (letter, lower-depth-profile) pairs have occurred.

The profile records which letters have appeared in which past contexts. For fixed kk, there are finitely many profiles, and higher profiles determine all lower ones by forgetting their deepest context layer. For k≥1k\geq 1,

Uk​(u​a)=Uk​(u)∪{(a,Uk−1​(u))}.U_{k}(ua)=U_{k}(u)\cup\{(a,U_{k-1}(u))\}. (37)

Thus profiles grow by inclusion and update deterministically from the next letter. Structural induction shows that (wi,Uk​(w<i))(w_{i},U_{k}(w_{<i})) determines every formula of past depth at most kk at position ii. At the virtual endpoint, all letter atoms are false, so Uk​(w)U_{k}(w) alone determines truth. Equal profiles therefore give equal residual languages.

Lemma D.2 (Counting strict profile changes).

For every k≥0k\geq 0, along the prefixes of any word, UkU_{k} changes at most

(k+ss)−1\binom{k+s}{s}-1 (38)

times. Consequently, if pd⁡(Ψ)≤k\operatorname{pd}(\Psi)\leq k, the reduced DFA of L⁡(Ψ)L(\Psi) has height at most (k+ss)−1\binom{k+s}{s}-1.

Proof.

For each a∈Σa\in\Sigma, define its next-change rank after uu by

ra​(u)=min⁡{j≥1:Uj​(u​a)≠Uj​(u)}.r_{a}(u)=\min\{j\geq 1:U_{j}(ua)\neq U_{j}(u)\}.

This is finite because 𝐏|u|+1⊤\mathbf{P}^{|u|+1}\top distinguishes uu from u​aua at the virtual endpoint. In particular,

Uk(ua)≠Uk(u)⟺ra(u)≤k.U_{k}(ua)\neq U_{k}(u)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_{a}(u)\leq k. (39)

Initially, ra​(ϵ)=1r_{a}({\epsilon})=1. If t=ra​(u)t=r_{a}(u), the ranks update as

ra(ua)=t+1,rb(ua)=min{rb(u),t+1}(b≠a).r_{a}(ua)=t+1,\qquad r_{b}(ua)=\min\{r_{b}(u),t+1\}\quad(b\neq a). (40)

A letter not yet seen has rank 11. Otherwise, comparing with the prefix before its last occurrence shows that its rank is one plus the first depth at which the intervening profiles differ. Appending aa changes profiles from depth tt onwards, which gives equation 40.

For fixed kk, let

ρk(u)≔sort(min{ra(u),k+1}:a∈Σ).\rho_{k}(u)\coloneqq\operatorname{sort}\bigl(\min\{r_{a}(u),k+1\}:a\in\Sigma\bigr).

If t≤kt\leq k, Equation equation 40 replaces one entry tt by t+1t+1, leaves all entries below tt fixed, and leaves every other altered entry at least t+1t+1. Hence

Uk(ua)≠Uk(u)⟹ρk(u)<lexρk(ua).U_{k}(ua)\neq U_{k}(u)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\rho_{k}(u)<_{\mathrm{lex}}\rho_{k}(ua).

If t>kt>k, both UkU_{k} and ρk\rho_{k} are unchanged. Since there are exactly

(k+ss)\binom{k+s}{s}

nondecreasing ss-tuples in {1,…,k+1}s\{1,\ldots,k+1\}^{s}, the profile changes at most (k+ss)−1\binom{k+s}{s}-1 times. The profile automaton recognises L⁡(Ψ)L(\Psi); reduction cannot increase its height. ∎

This counts profile changes along a run, not the total number of profiles.

Lemma D.3 (Past depth of transformer outputs).

Under the stated assumptions, a transformer T∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(L,D,H)T\in\mathcal{FPT}(L,D,H) with output dimension ν\nu admits coordinate/value formulas Φd,fT∈LTL​[P]\Phi^{T}_{d,f}\in\textbf{LTL}[\textbf{P}] satisfying

w,i⊧Φd,fT⇔T​(w)d,i=f,pd⁡(Φd,fT)≤r𝔽​L,w,i\models\Phi^{T}_{d,f}\iff T(w)_{d,i}=f,\qquad\operatorname{pd}(\Phi^{T}_{d,f})\leq r_{\mathbb{F}}L,

for every 1≤i≤|w|1\leq i\leq|w|, 1≤d≤ν1\leq d\leq\nu, and f∈𝔽f\in\mathbb{F}.

Proof.

In the construction of Lemma D.1, embeddings have depth zero and pointwise maps do not increase depth. At each layer, the unary key/value predicates inherit the previous layer’s depth. Counting their occurrences up to r𝔽r_{\mathbb{F}} adds at most r𝔽r_{\mathbb{F}} nested past operators; attention then uses only Boolean combinations of these tests and the current query predicates. Each layer therefore increases depth by at most r𝔽r_{\mathbb{F}}. ∎

Corollary D.2.

Put L∗=max⁡{Ls,Lt}L_{*}=\max\{L_{s},L_{t}\}. The reduced poDFA 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} of the difference function satisfies

ht⁡(𝒜Δ)≤(r𝔽​L∗+ss).\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}_{\Delta})\leq\binom{r_{\mathbb{F}}L_{*}+s}{s}. (41)
Proof.

Set k=r𝔽​L∗k=r_{\mathbb{F}}L_{*}. Using the output formulas of Lemma D.3 in equation 32 gives pd⁡(ψΔ)≤k\operatorname{pd}(\psi_{\Delta})\leq k. Construct a DFA that stores Uk​(u)U_{k}(u) until the first mismatch. On reading aa, (a,Uk​(u))(a,U_{k}(u)) determines ψΔ\psi_{\Delta} at the new position: if true, enter an accepting absorbing state; otherwise update UkU_{k}. This recognises L⁡(ΨΔ)L(\Psi_{\Delta}).

The profile grows by inclusion, so the DFA is partially ordered. Lemma D.2 allows at most (k+ss)−1\binom{k+s}{s}-1 profile changes, and entering the accepting state adds at most one. Reduction preserves partial order and cannot increase height. ∎

For fixed Σ\Sigma and 𝔽\mathbb{F}, this bound is polynomial in L∗L_{*}, of degree s=|Σ|s=|\Sigma|, and independent of widths, head counts, and output dimension. It bounds automaton height, not the size of the representing formulas.

Remark D.3 (Mealy-machine interpretation).

The same profile Ur𝔽​L​(u)U_{r_{\mathbb{F}}L}(u), together with the next letter, determines all outputs of TT. It therefore also realises TT as a Mealy machine, giving

ht⁡(ℳT)≤(r𝔽​L+ss)−1.\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{M}_{T})\leq\binom{r_{\mathbb{F}}L+s}{s}-1. (42)

Summing the two individual bounds via equation 35 also bounds ht⁡(𝒜Δ)\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}_{\Delta}). The poDFA proof above is sharper because both transformers share Ur𝔽​L∗U_{r_{\mathbb{F}}L_{*}} on their common input.

Remark D.4.

We remark that Masopust and Thomazo (2015) showed a related bound (also in terms of a binomial coefficient) on the height of the minimal DFA representing piecewise testable languages; such languages are expressible by fixed-precision transformers. Our result differs in applying to difference automata for general fixed-precision transformers, and in expressing the bound in terms of the size parameters of those transformers.

D.3 Deterministic length generalization

Either height bound from Corollary D.1-D.2 gives a deterministic length cutoff: any nonzero difference function between two transformers has its behaviour controlled by height of its poDFA. Taking the smaller bound yields the following result.

Lemma D.4 (Deterministic length generalization).

Let Ts∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(Ls,Ds,Hs)T_{s}\in\mathcal{FPT}(L_{s},D_{s},H_{s}) and Tt∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(Lt,Dt,Ht)T_{t}\in\mathcal{FPT}(L_{t},D_{t},H_{t}) satisfy the preceding hypotheses, with Ls≥LtL_{s}\geq L_{t} as in Remark 2.1. Using the arithmetic constant r𝔽r_{\mathbb{F}} from Appendix B.2, set

C0:=r𝔽​[Ls​Ds​|𝔽|Dh,s+1+Lt​Dt​|𝔽|Dh,t+1]+1,C1:=(r𝔽​Ls+|Σ||Σ|).C_{0}:=r_{\mathbb{F}}\left[L_{s}D_{s}|\mathbb{F}|^{D_{h,s}+1}+L_{t}D_{t}|\mathbb{F}|^{D_{h,t}+1}\right]+1,\qquad C_{1}:=\binom{r_{\mathbb{F}}L_{s}+|\Sigma|}{|\Sigma|}. (43)

For C:=min⁡{C0,C1}C:=\min\{C_{0},C_{1}\}, agreement on all words of length at most CC implies agreement on every word:

Ts|≤C≡Tt|≤C⟹Ts≡Tt.T_{s}|_{\leq C}\equiv T_{t}|_{\leq C}\quad\implies\quad T_{s}\equiv T_{t}.
Proof.

Corollaries D.1 and D.2 give ht⁡(𝒜Δ)≤min⁡{C0,C1}=C\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}_{\Delta})\leq\min\{C_{0},C_{1}\}=C. If Ts≢TtT_{s}\not\equiv T_{t}, let ww be a shortest word accepted by 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta}. Its run contains no self-loop as deleting the corresponding letter would give a shorter accepted word. Every letter therefore induces a strict transition, so |w|≤ht⁡(𝒜Δ)≤C|w|\leq\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}_{\Delta})\leq C, contradicting agreement on Σ≤C\Sigma^{\leq C}. ∎

D.4 Probabilistic length generalization

We now show that low error up to a sufficiently large cutoff persists at all larger lengths. The argument is automata-theoretic: a random input makes uniformly positive progress through a partially ordered DFA until it reaches an absorbing state.

Let 𝒜=(Q,Σ,δ,q0,B)\mathcal{A}=(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_{0},B) be a partially ordered DFA, with bad states B⊆QB\subseteq Q, and let s=|Σ|≥2s=|\Sigma|\geq 2. Let C≥0C\geq 0 be an integer upper bound on ht⁡(𝒜)\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}). For the difference function, take 𝒜=𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{\Delta}, with BB its accepting states and C=min⁡{C0,C1}C=\min\{C_{0},C_{1}\} from equation 43. For an exact length mm, and for the distribution uniform over all words of length at most KK, respectively, write

pm≔Prw∼Unif⁡(Σm)[δ(q0,w)∈B],𝒟K≔Unif(Σ≤K),eK≔Prw∼𝒟K[δ(q0,w)∈B].p_{m}\coloneqq\Pr_{w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{m})}[\delta(q_{0},w)\in B],\qquad\mathcal{D}_{K}\coloneqq\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{\leq K}),\qquad e_{K}\coloneqq\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{K}}[\delta(q_{0},w)\in B].

Thus pmp_{m} is the bad-state probability at one fixed length, whereas eKe_{K} is the bad-state probability when every word of length at most KK is equally likely. The mass that 𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{K} assigns to length KK is

λK≔Prw∼𝒟K[|w|=K]=sK1+s+⋯+sK=(s−1)​sKsK+1−1>s−1s.\lambda_{K}\coloneqq\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{K}}[|w|=K]=\frac{s^{K}}{1+s+\cdots+s^{K}}=\frac{(s-1)s^{K}}{s^{K+1}-1}>\frac{s-1}{s}.

Write QabsQ_{\mathrm{abs}} for the absorbing states of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, namely those satisfying δ⁡(q,a)=q\delta(q,a)=q for every a∈Σa\in\Sigma. All other states are called transient.

Lemma D.5 (Absorption tail).

Let 0<ϵ<10<{\epsilon}<1. If

K≥s⁡(C+log⁡1ϵ+log2⁡1ϵ+2​C​log⁡1ϵ),K\geq s\left(C+\log\frac{1}{{\epsilon}}+\sqrt{\log^{2}\frac{1}{{\epsilon}}+2C\log\frac{1}{{\epsilon}}}\right),

then a uniformly random word WK∈ΣKW_{K}\in\Sigma^{K} ends in a transient state with probability at most ϵ{\epsilon}.

Proof.

If C=0C=0, the initial state is absorbing and the claim is immediate. At every transient state, at least one letter makes a strict transition. Count a step as successful if it makes a strict transition or the run was already absorbed. Each step has conditional success probability at least 1/s1/s, so sequential coupling shows that the total success count stochastically dominates Y∼Bin⁡(K,1/s)Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(K,1/s). If the run is still transient after KK steps, all successes were strict transitions and there were fewer than CC of them. Hence

Pr[δ(q0,WK)∉Qabs]≤Pr[Y<C].\Pr[\delta(q_{0},W_{K})\notin Q_{\mathrm{abs}}]\leq\Pr[Y<C].

We use Chernoff’s inequality to obtain an explicit sufficient cutoff.

Put μ=K/s\mu=K/s and ℓϵ=log⁡(1/ϵ)\ell_{\epsilon}=\log(1/{\epsilon}). The displayed condition implies μ>C\mu>C. With η=1−C/μ∈(0,1)\eta=1-C/\mu\in(0,1), the multiplicative Chernoff lower-tail bound11 1 See Wikipedia, “Chernoff bound: Multiplicative form (relative error)”. gives

Pr[Y<C]≤Pr[Y≤(1−η)μ]≤exp(−μ​η22)=exp(−(μ−C)22​μ).\Pr[Y<C]\leq\Pr[Y\leq(1-\eta)\mu]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\mu\eta^{2}}{2}\right)=\exp\left(-\frac{(\mu-C)^{2}}{2\mu}\right).

It remains to make the exponent at least ℓϵ\ell_{\epsilon}. This is equivalent to

μ2−2​(C+ℓϵ)​μ+C2≥0.\mu^{2}-2(C+\ell_{\epsilon})\mu+C^{2}\geq 0.

The larger root of the left-hand quadratic is

C+ℓϵ+ℓϵ2+2​C​ℓϵ.C+\ell_{\epsilon}+\sqrt{\ell_{\epsilon}^{2}+2C\ell_{\epsilon}}.

Condition (P) is exactly the assertion that μ\mu is at least this root. Hence (μ−C)2/(2​μ)≥ℓϵ(\mu-C)^{2}/(2\mu)\geq\ell_{\epsilon}, and the preceding display is at most e−ℓϵ=ϵe^{-\ell_{\epsilon}}={\epsilon}. ∎

Theorem D.1 (Probabilistic length generalization).

Let 0<ϵ<10<{\epsilon}<1. Suppose that KK satisfies (P) and that

Prw∼Unif⁡(Σ≤K)[δ(q0,w)∈B]≤ϵ.\Pr_{w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{\leq K})}[\delta(q_{0},w)\in B]\leq{\epsilon}.

Then the probability of reaching a bad state remains small both at every fixed length m≥Km\geq K and over all words of length at most M≥KM\geq K:

Prw∼Unif⁡(Σm)[δ(q0,w)∈B]<3ϵ,Prw∼Unif⁡(Σ≤M)[δ(q0,w)∈B]<3ϵ.\Pr_{w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{m})}[\delta(q_{0},w)\in B]<3{\epsilon},\qquad\Pr_{w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{\leq M})}[\delta(q_{0},w)\in B]<3{\epsilon}.
Proof.

The bad absorbing states at time KK account for at most the bad probability conditioned on length KK. Hence

Pr[δ(q0,WK)∈B∩Qabs]≤pK≤eKλK<ss−1ϵ≤2ϵ.\Pr[\delta(q_{0},W_{K})\in B\cap Q_{\mathrm{abs}}]\leq p_{K}\leq\frac{e_{K}}{\lambda_{K}}<\frac{s}{s-1}{\epsilon}\leq 2{\epsilon}.

By Lemma D.5, the run is still transient at time KK with probability at most ϵ{\epsilon}. If a word of length m>Km>K ends in a bad state, then at time KK its run was either transient or already in a bad absorbing state. Therefore, by (A),

pm\displaystyle p_{m} ≤pK+Pr[δ(q0,WK)∉Qabs]\displaystyle\leq p_{K}+\Pr[\delta(q_{0},W_{K})\notin Q_{\mathrm{abs}}]
<2​ϵ⏟from ​eK≤ϵ+ϵ⏟absorption tail=3ϵ(m>K).\displaystyle<\underbrace{2{\epsilon}}_{\text{from }e_{K}\leq{\epsilon}}+\underbrace{{\epsilon}}_{\text{absorption tail}}=3{\epsilon}\qquad(m>K).

The same bound holds for m=Km=K by (A). Finally, eMe_{M} is a weighted average of eKe_{K} and the fixed-length errors pK+1,…,pMp_{K+1},\ldots,p_{M}; each of these terms is strictly below 3​ϵ3{\epsilon}. Thus eM<3​ϵe_{M}<3{\epsilon}. ∎

Remark D.5.

Keeping the alphabet dependence in the proof gives pm,eM<(2+1/(s−1))​ϵp_{m},e_{M}<(2+1/(s-1)){\epsilon}. The upper-bound coefficient is 33 for binary alphabets and approaches 22 as ss grows; this does not assert that the bound is attained.

D.5 Dependence of Chain Length on L and 𝔽\mathbb{F}

We construct difference functions with unbounded poDFA height by varying either precision or depth, with the other architectural sizes fixed. Throughout, Σ={a}\Sigma=\{a\}, and outputs are scalar.

Implementation convention.

Both constructions use one head and arithmetic satisfying Appendix B.2, with attention sums rounded after summation.

To select specific positions with attention, we operate the following way. Choose a negative score z∈𝔽z\in\mathbb{F} such that exp⁡(z)\exp(z) rounds to zero. In particular, setting the convention that ∞⋅0=0\infty\cdot 0=0, zz can take the value −∞-\infty. Selected positions then receive score 00 while unselected positions receive score zz and value 00. Thus attention averages the selected values unless the denominator overflows.

Both constructions keep track of a fixed number of Boolean values, such as whether a position is selected. We represent each Boolean value using two coordinates: (1,0)(1,0) for true and (0,1)(0,1) for false. A separate coordinate stores the attention output.

D.5.1 Necessity of precision dependence

We create a family of framework where we increase precision while keeping both transformer architectures fixed. For each sufficiently large integer kk, use the precision set

𝔽k={0,±∞}∪{±j,±1/j:1≤j≤k}∪𝒞k.\mathbb{F}_{k}=\{0,\pm\infty\}\cup\{\pm j,\pm 1/j:1\leq j\leq k\}\cup\mathcal{C}_{k}.

Here 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} contains a bounded number of additional values needed for the attention scores and the Boolean encoding above, including its pointwise computations. Thus pk≔|𝔽k|=4​k+O⁡(1)p_{k}\coloneqq|\mathbb{F}_{k}|=4k+O(1) grows linearly with kk. Choose the arithmetic so that positive attention sums exceeding kk overflow to +∞+\infty. Increasing kk therefore allows uniform attention to average more positions before overflowing.

Proposition D.2 (Precision can force linear height growth).

For the precision structures 𝔽k\mathbb{F}_{k} above, there are pairs of transformers with fixed depths Ls=Lt=2L_{s}=L_{t}=2, fixed widths, and Hs=Ht=1H_{s}=H_{t}=1, whose reduced difference poDFAs satisfy

ht⁡(𝒜Δk)=k+2=Θ⁡(pk).\operatorname{ht}(\mathcal{A}_{\Delta_{k}})=k+2=\Theta(p_{k}).

Thus the height can grow linearly with precision-set size while the architectures and alphabet remain fixed.

Proof.

Both transformers first apply uniform attention with value 11 at every position. The resulting bit is

b(i)=𝟏{2≤i≤k+1}.b(i)=\mathbf{1}\{2\leq i\leq k+1\}.

The teacher retains this bit through its second block. The student’s second block attends only to earlier positions with b⁡(j)=1b(j)=1, using value b⁡(j)b(j), and takes the Boolean OR with the current bit. At most kk positions are selected, so this attention never overflows. Consequently,

Tt(w)i=𝟏{2≤i≤k+1},Ts(w)i=𝟏{i≥2},Δk(w)=𝟏{|w|≥k+2}.T_{t}(w)_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{2\leq i\leq k+1\},\qquad T_{s}(w)_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{i\geq 2\},\qquad\Delta_{k}(w)=\mathbf{1}\{|w|\geq k+2\}.

The reduced DFA of {w:|w|≥m}\{w:|w|\geq m\} counts length up to mm, then remains in an accepting sink. Its m+1m+1 states are distinct: counts r<t≤mr<t\leq m are distinguished by a suffix of length m−tm-t. Its height is therefore mm, giving k+2k+2 here. Only Boolean attention outputs occur in this construction, so the encoding and feed-forward width are independent of kk. Their pointwise computations and the score maps require only a bounded number of additional scalar values, as claimed for 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k}. ∎

Thus no height bound over arbitrary precision structures can ignore its precision set cardinality |𝔽||\mathbb{F}|.

D.5.2 Necessity of linear depth dependence

Proposition D.3.

For one fixed precision structure 𝔽\mathbb{F}, there are transformers TmT_{m} of depth L=2​mL=2m, with fixed width and one head, whose difference poDFAs against an always-zero transformer have height m=L/2m=L/2.

Proof.

Fix a cutoff k≥2k\geq 2 and an adequate arithmetic with the same overflow as in the previous proposition. Its two-layer student computes 𝟏{i≥2}\mathbf{1}\{i\geq 2\}. Taking the complement gives a marker u1(i)=𝟏{i=1}u_{1}(i)=\mathbf{1}\{i=1\}.

Two further layers move a unique marker forward by one position. Indeed, suppose

uj(i)=𝟏{i=j}.u_{j}(i)=\mathbf{1}\{i=j\}.

Thus, uju_{j} is 11 only at position jj.

The first added layer records whether the marker has appeared at the current position or earlier:

sj(i)=uj(i)∨𝟏{an earlier marker exists}=𝟏{i≥j}.s_{j}(i)=u_{j}(i)\vee\mathbf{1}\{\text{an earlier marker exists}\}=\mathbf{1}\{i\geq j\}.

The second layer attends uniformly to the earlier positions selected by sjs_{j}. At position i>ji>j, these are the positions j,j+1,…,i−1j,j+1,\ldots,i-1. But only position jj has value uj=1u_{j}=1; all other selected positions have value 00. Hence the attention output is

rj​(i)={1/(i−j),1≤i−j≤k,0,otherwise.r_{j}(i)=\begin{cases}1/(i-j),&1\leq i-j\leq k,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

In particular, rj​(i)=1r_{j}(i)=1 holds exactly when i=j+1i=j+1. Setting

uj+1(i)=𝟏{rj(i)=1}u_{j+1}(i)=\mathbf{1}\{r_{j}(i)=1\}

therefore creates a unique marker at position j+1j+1. This shift uses fixed parameters and can be repeated for every jj.

Starting from u1u_{1}, and applying m−1m-1 shifts, uses 2​m2m layers and gives

Tm(w)i=𝟏{i=m},Δm(w)=𝟏{|w|≥m}.T_{m}(w)_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{i=m\},\qquad\Delta_{m}(w)=\mathbf{1}\{|w|\geq m\}.

∎

With 𝔽\mathbb{F}, Σ\Sigma, DD, and HH fixed, this proposition proves the necessity in, at least, a linear dependence on depth in the bound on the height of a difference transformer.

Appendix E Data Complexity Bound

This appendix collects the statistical (in-distribution) generalization bound underlying Proposition 4.1. The core argument is imported from Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026), which studies the same student–teacher setting for single-output transformers; in order to keep the present paper self-contained, we restate the main result in our notation and sketch its proof (Appendix E.1), pointing the reader to Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026) for full details. We then describe the two modifications needed for our setting, stemming from the absence of attention output projection matrices in our transformers (Appendix E.2) and the fact our transformers produce vectorial outputs at every position (Appendix E.3). Furthermore, we contrast the resulting G&C bound with the analogous bound for ERM (Appendix E.4) and discuss the statistical bounds on transformer architectures that include attention score rescaling or layer norm (Appendix E.5).

Throughout, we write Dh,s:=Ds/HsD_{h,s}:=D_{s}/H_{s} and Dh,t:=Dt/HtD_{h,t}:=D_{t}/H_{t} for the per-head dimensions, and Dff,s,Dff,tD_{\mathrm{ff},s},D_{\mathrm{ff},t} for the hidden widths of the feed-forward blocks. All parameters take values in the finite set 𝔽\mathbb{F}, so that a transformer in ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(L,D,H)\mathcal{FPT}(L,D,H) has finitely many configurations and G&C samples uniformly among them.

E.1 Main statement and proof sketch

We say that a student TsT_{s} is teacher-equivalent (TE) to TtT_{t} on 𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{K} if Prw∼𝒟K[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)]=0\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{K}}[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)]=0. Let p~\tilde{p} denote the probability that a uniformly random Ts∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(Ls,Ds,Hs)T_{s}\in\mathcal{FPT}(L_{s},D_{s},H_{s}) is TE. The following is the general form of the G&C bound, as given by  Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026), where the considered transformer class ℱ​𝒫​𝒯~\widetilde{\mathcal{FPT}} uses output projection matrices after attention, and assumes only one output value per word instead of our vectorial outputs at every position.

Theorem E.1 (Statistical generalization for G&C; adapted from Theorem B.1 and Corollary B.1 of Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026)).

Fix ϵ∈(0,1){\epsilon}\in(0,1) and δ∈(0,15)\delta\in(0,\tfrac{1}{5}). Let Tt∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯~​(Lt,Dt,Ht)T_{t}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{FPT}}(L_{t},D_{t},H_{t}) be a teacher and ℋ=ℱ​𝒫​𝒯~​(Ls,Ds,Hs)\mathcal{H}=\widetilde{\mathcal{FPT}}(L_{s},D_{s},H_{s}) a hypothesis class with

Ls≥Lt,Ds≥Dt,Hs≥Ht,Dh,s≥Dh,t,Dff,s≥Dff,t.L_{s}\geq L_{t},\qquad D_{s}\geq D_{t},\qquad H_{s}\geq H_{t},\qquad D_{h,s}\geq D_{h,t},\qquad D_{\mathrm{ff},s}\geq D_{\mathrm{ff},t}.

Then

p~≥|𝔽|−B,\tilde{p}\;\geq\;|\mathbb{F}|^{-B},

where

B:=\displaystyle B\;:=\; |Σ|​Ds+Lt​(Ht​(Dt​Dh,t+2​Dt​Dh,s)CLOSE\displaystyle|\Sigma|D_{s}\;+\;L_{t}\Big(H_{t}\big(D_{t}D_{h,t}+2D_{t}D_{h,s}\big)
OPEN+(Hs−Ht)​Dt​Dh,s+Ds​Dt+Ds​Dff,t+Dt​Dff,s+Ds+Dff,s)\displaystyle+\ \ \ \ \ (H_{s}-H_{t})\,D_{t}D_{h,s}+D_{s}D_{t}+D_{s}D_{\mathrm{ff},t}+D_{t}D_{\mathrm{ff},s}+D_{s}+D_{\mathrm{ff},s}\Big)
+(Ls−Lt)​(Hs​Dh,s+Dff,s+1)​Dt.\displaystyle+\;(L_{s}-L_{t})\big(H_{s}D_{h,s}+D_{\mathrm{ff},s}+1\big)D_{t}.

Consequently, if TsT_{s} is obtained by the G&C learner on an i.i.d. sample SS of NN strings from 𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{K} with

N≥1ϵ​(B​log⁡|𝔽|+3​log⁡(2/δ)),N\;\geq\;\frac{1}{{\epsilon}}\big(B\log|\mathbb{F}|+3\log(2/\delta)\big),

then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over SS and the draw of TsT_{s},

Prw∼𝒟K[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)]<ϵ.\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{K}}\big[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)\big]<{\epsilon}.

One then has B∼𝒪⁡(Lt​Dt2+Ds​Dt​(Ls+Lt)+|Σ|​Ds)B\sim\mathcal{O}\big(L_{t}D_{t}^{2}+D_{s}D_{t}(L_{s}+L_{t})+|\Sigma|D_{s}\big) under the standard conventions D=H​DhD=HD_{h} and Dff=DD_{\mathrm{ff}}=D.

The output matrices term Lt​Ds​DtL_{t}D_{s}D_{t} is removed from BB in Appendix E.2 and the readout term required for per-position outputs is added in Appendix E.3; Proposition 4.1 is the combination of Theorem E.1 with these two modifications and with the ERM bound of Appendix E.4.

Proof sketch.

The proof has two ingredients.

From p~\tilde{p} to a sample-complexity bound.

The main lemma of Buzaglo et al. (2024) states that, for any finite hypothesis class and any 0/10/1 loss, if the probability of sampling a TE hypothesis under the prior is p~<12\tilde{p}<\tfrac{1}{2}, then G&C generalizes to error below ϵ{\epsilon} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta as soon as N≥(−log⁡p~+3​log⁡(2/δ))/ϵN\geq(-\log\tilde{p}+3\log(2/\delta))/{\epsilon}. Hence it suffices to lower bound p~\tilde{p}, and p~≥|𝔽|−B\tilde{p}\geq|\mathbb{F}|^{-B} yields the stated bound.

Lower bounding p~\tilde{p} by constraint counting.

We exhibit one explicit set of BB parameter values such that any student agreeing with them on those BB coordinates (and arbitrary elsewhere) computes exactly the function of TtT_{t}. Since parameters are drawn uniformly from 𝔽\mathbb{F}, this event has probability exactly |𝔽|−B|\mathbb{F}|^{-B}, and p~\tilde{p} is at least as large. The construction proceeds layer by layer and maintains the invariant that, at every position, the residual stream of the student has the form [λ⋆,𝟎][\lambda^{\star},\mathbf{0}], where λ⋆∈𝔽Dt\lambda^{\star}\in\mathbb{F}^{D_{t}} is the residual stream of the teacher and the remaining Ds−DtD_{s}-D_{t} coordinates are zero.

  • •

    Embedding. The first embedding coordinates of every token are given by the teacher’s embedding, and the bottom Ds−DtD_{s}-D_{t} coordinates are set to zero; this contributes |Σ|​Ds|\Sigma|D_{s} constraints.

  • •

    Teacher layers (ℓ≤Lt\ell\leq L_{t}). For each of the HtH_{t} teacher heads, the top-left Dt×Dh,tD_{t}\times D_{h,t} blocks of the student’s 𝐖Q,𝐖K,𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V} are set to the teacher’s matrices, and the blocks of 𝐖Q,𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{V} acting on the extra head coordinates are set to zero; since the query is zero on these coordinates, 𝐖K\mathbf{W}_{K} may be left free there. For the remaining Hs−HtH_{s}-H_{t} heads only the top block of 𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{V} is zeroed, so that they contribute nothing to the teacher coordinates. The output projection and the feed-forward block are constrained analogously: their teacher blocks are copied and the blocks that would leak into (or read from) the extra coordinates are zeroed, including the biases. This preserves the invariant and contributes the Lt​(⋅)L_{t}(\cdot) term of BB; see Lemma B.2 of Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026) for the block matrices.

  • •

    Weak-identity layers (Lt<ℓ≤LsL_{t}<\ell\leq L_{s}). The extra Ls−LtL_{s}-L_{t} layers need only preserve the top DtD_{t} coordinates, not the full residual. Setting the first DtD_{t} columns of the attention output projection, of the second feed-forward matrix, and of the corresponding bias to zero suffices; the bottom coordinates may then take arbitrary values without affecting the teacher block. This contributes (Hs​Dh,s+Dff,s+1)​Dt(H_{s}D_{h,s}+D_{\mathrm{ff},s}+1)D_{t} constraints per layer, which is the last term of BB (Theorem B.1 of Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026)).

Summing the three contributions gives BB, and the asymptotic form follows by substituting D=H​DhD=HD_{h} and Dff=DD_{\mathrm{ff}}=D. ∎

E.2 Absence of output projection matrices

Unlike the architecture in Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026), neither our teacher nor our student has an attention output projection. In the first LtL_{t} layers, there is therefore no output matrix to copy or pad with zeros. This removes Ds​DtD_{s}D_{t} constraints per layer.

For each of the remaining Ls−LtL_{s}-L_{t} weak-identity layers, the source construction zeros the part of the output projection that writes to the teacher coordinates. We instead zero the rows of the value matrices 𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{V} that produce these coordinates. There are DtD_{t} such rows in total, each with DsD_{s} entries. The residual connection then preserves the DtD_{t} first dimensions, and the count of fixed parameters on this layers is exactly as before.

We hence have for this distinction, a reduced constraint count

Bno​-​proj=B−Lt​Ds​Dt.B_{\mathrm{no\text{-}proj}}=B-L_{t}D_{s}D_{t}.

E.3 Per-position outputs

Theorem E.1 is stated for a single output per string, as in Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026). transformers in ℱ​𝒫​𝒯\mathcal{FPT} instead return a vector of dimension ν\nu at every position through the pointwise affine output layer O\operatorname{O} (Definition 2.1). We write 𝐔∈𝔽ν×Ds\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu\times D_{s}} and 𝐮∈𝔽ν\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu} for the student’s output weights and bias, and 𝐔⋆∈𝔽ν×Dt\mathbf{U}^{\star}\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu\times D_{t}}, 𝐮⋆∈𝔽ν\mathbf{u}^{\star}\in\mathbb{F}^{\nu} for the teacher’s. Teacher-equivalence is understood in the strict per-string sense: TsT_{s} is TE if, with probability one over w∼𝒟Kw\sim\mathcal{D}_{K}, its output matches the teacher’s at every position. The corresponding empirical loss on a sample (w(n))n≤N(w^{(n)})_{n\leq N} is

1N∑n=1N𝕀[∃i≤|w(n)|:Ts(w(n))i≠Tt(w(n))i],\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}\Big[\exists\,i\leq|w^{(n)}|\;:\;T_{s}(w^{(n)})_{i}\neq T_{t}(w^{(n)})_{i}\Big],

which is {0,1}\{0,1\}-valued per string and therefore fits the G&C lemma of Buzaglo et al. (2024) without change.

The constraint-counting argument carries over verbatim: the construction of Appendix E.1 preserves the teacher’s residual stream in the top DtD_{t} coordinates at every position, not only at the last one. The only additional constraints come from the output layer. Writing the student’s final residual stream at position ii as [λi⋆,λ~i][\lambda_{i}^{\star},\tilde{\lambda}_{i}], matching the teacher’s output at every position requires the first DtD_{t} columns of 𝐔\mathbf{U} to equal 𝐔⋆\mathbf{U}^{\star}, the remaining Ds−DtD_{s}-D_{t} columns to be zero (so that λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i} does not leak into the output), and 𝐮=𝐮⋆\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}^{\star}. This fixes every entry of the output layer, adding exactly (Ds+1)​ν(D_{s}+1)\,\nu constraints, so that the constraint count becomes

Bseq=Bno​-​proj+(Ds+1)​ν.B_{\mathrm{seq}}\;=\;B_{\mathrm{no\text{-}proj}}\;+\;(D_{s}+1)\,\nu.

Since ν\nu is fixed by the task, this term is subleading whenever ν≤Dt\nu\leq D_{t}, and the asymptotics of Theorem E.1 are unchanged.

E.4 Comparison to ERM

An analogous sample-complexity bound holds under Empirical Risk Minimization, obtained by a standard uniform-convergence argument over the finite hypothesis class ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(Ls,Ds,Hs,𝔽)\mathcal{FPT}(L_{s},D_{s},H_{s},\mathbb{F}) (Appendix B.1 of Buzaglo et al. (2024)). Counting parameters layer by layer under Ds=Hs​Dh,sD_{s}=H_{s}D_{h,s} and Dff,s=DsD_{\mathrm{ff},s}=D_{s} (|Σ|​Ds|\Sigma|D_{s} for the embedding layer, 3​Hs​Ds​Dh,s=3​Ds23H_{s}D_{s}D_{h,s}=3D_{s}^{2} for the query, key and value matrices, 2​Ds22D_{s}^{2} for the two feed-forward matrices, and 2​Ds2D_{s} for the biases), the total parameter count of the student, and hence the ERM complexity term, is

BE​R​M=|Σ|​Ds+Ls​(5​Ds2+2​Ds)+(Ds+1)​ν∼𝒪⁡(|Σ|​Ds+Ls​Ds2),B_{ERM}\;=\;|\Sigma|D_{s}+L_{s}\big(5D_{s}^{2}+2D_{s}\big)+(D_{s}+1)\,\nu\;\sim\;\mathcal{O}\big(|\Sigma|D_{s}\;+\;L_{s}D_{s}^{2}\big),

so that ERM generalizes to error below ϵ{\epsilon} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta whenever

N≥1ϵ​(BE​R​M​log⁡|𝔽|+log⁡(1/δ)).N\;\geq\;\frac{1}{{\epsilon}}\big(B_{ERM}\log|\mathbb{F}|+\log(1/\delta)\big).

Contrasting this with B≈𝒪⁡(Ls​Ds​Dt)B\approx\mathcal{O}(L_{s}D_{s}D_{t}) from Theorem E.1, ERM scales with the square of the student width, whereas G&C scales with the product of the student and teacher widths; when the teacher is genuinely narrow (Dt≪DsD_{t}\ll D_{s}), G&C therefore saves a factor on the order of Ds/DtD_{s}/D_{t} over ERM. This narrow-teacher advantage is intrinsic to the volume-based argument underlying G&C, and is not captured by capacity-based bounds (Edelman et al., 2022; Trauger and Tewari, 2024; Yang et al., 2026c).

E.5 Normalization within transformers in fixed precision

Our transformer model is inspired by Li and Cotterell (2025), but omits the attention-score factor 1/Dh1/\sqrt{D_{h}} and post layer normalization (Ba et al., 2016). Layer normalization and attention-score scaling can be seamlessly included in the ERM analysis of Appendix E.4. The argument counts the parameters of a finite hypothesis class and does not require a teacher–student embedding. Under the same realizability assumption, it is enough to include the learned normalization parameters in this count. As their number is linear in Ls​DsL_{s}D_{s}, the leading order of the ERM bound 𝒪⁡(Ls​Ds2+|Σ|​Ds)\mathcal{O}\big(L_{s}D_{s}^{2}+|\Sigma|D_{s}\big) is unchanged.

Accounting for this factor and the normalization in the constructive Guess & Check argument of Rizvi-Martel et al. (2026) would require extra technical conditions on the fixed-precision arithmetic; by omitting them, we keep the assumptions on 𝔽\mathbb{F} simple. The same counting method applies with normalization whenever the embedding preserves the teacher’s computation exactly. But since both normalizations depend on the model dimensions, the embedding of the teacher in a larger student requires additional conditions on the fixed-precision arithmetic, as described below.

Attention-score scaling.

The embedding pads the teacher’s queries and keys with zeros to preserve their dot product. With attention-score scaling, the teacher and student divide this product by Dh,t\sqrt{D_{h,t}} and Dh,s\sqrt{D_{h,s}}, respectively. In infinite-precision arithmetic, these factors can be matched by rescaling the copied query projection matrix:

WQ⋆⟼c​WQ⋆,c=Dh,s/Dh,t.W_{Q}^{\star}\longmapsto cW_{Q}^{\star},\qquad c=\sqrt{D_{h,s}/D_{h,t}}.

To use this rescaling in fixed precision, every entry of c​WQ⋆cW_{Q}^{\star} must belong to 𝔽\mathbb{F}. Representability of cc is needed, but is not enough, as rounding within the projections, dot products, and score division can break the equality. Additional assumptions are hence required, ensuring that this rescaling preserves the rounded scores and controls the overflow and underflow.

Layer normalization.

For a vector xx, layer normalization takes the form

LN⁡(x)=γ⊙x−μ⁡(x)​𝟏v⁡(x)+ϵLN+β,\operatorname{LN}(x)=\gamma\odot\frac{x-\mu(x)\mathbf{1}}{\sqrt{v(x)+\epsilon_{\mathrm{LN}}}}+\beta,

where μ⁡(x)\mu(x) and v⁡(x)v(x) are the mean and variance across coordinates, γ\gamma and β\beta are learned vectors, and ϵLN\epsilon_{\mathrm{LN}} is a stabilization constant. Absorbing this operation into the embedding requires accounting for the mean and variance of the added coordinates. Writing zero padding as x¯=[x;0]∈ℝDs\bar{x}=[x;0]\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{s}} for x∈ℝDtx\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{t}} and a=Dt/Dsa=D_{t}/D_{s}, we have in infinite-precision arithmetic,

μ⁡(x¯)=a​μ​(x),v⁡(x¯)=a​v​(x)+a⁡(1−a)​μ​(x)2.\mu(\bar{x})=a\mu(x),\qquad v(\bar{x})=av(x)+a(1-a)\mu(x)^{2}.

The change thus depends on the input xx, and cannot generally be corrected by fixed γ\gamma and β\beta. More elaborate padding schemes would need to preserve the teacher’s normalized coordinates through every sublayer. Any compensating parameters must also be representable in 𝔽\mathbb{F}, and the correction must survive rounding for every residual vector the teacher can produce. Extra student layers pose a further problem: setting their attention and feed-forward to zero still leaves layer normalization acting on the residual. Thus, including layer normalization in the construction requires conditions on both the encoding and the arithmetic. Given the technical complexity, we prefer to formalize transformers without layer normalization for our results.

Remark E.1.

These constraints concern our particular construction (Appendix E.1), rather than G&C itself. For ERM, the statistical bound applies directly to the normalized architecture, and Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.2 hold with the updated ERM statistical bound.

Appendix F Main theorem and Tradeoff

F.1 Main theorem

The main result given by Theorem 4.1 simply combines two results: sufficiently many samples give small error on 𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{K}, and a sufficiently large cutoff KK extends that guarantee to every 𝒟M\mathcal{D}_{M} with M≥KM\geq K.

Theorem F.1.

Fix ϵ∈(0,1){\epsilon}\in(0,1), δ∈(0,15)\delta\in(0,\tfrac{1}{5}), and |Σ|≥2|\Sigma|\geq 2. Let the student Ts∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(Ls,Ds,Hs)T_{s}\in\mathcal{FPT}(L_{s},D_{s},H_{s}) and teacher Tt∈ℱ​𝒫​𝒯​(Lt,Dt,Ht)T_{t}\in\mathcal{FPT}(L_{t},D_{t},H_{t}) satisfy the learning framework of Remark 2.1, and the arithmetic assumptions of Appendix B.2. Let BB be an admissible G&C complexity term from Proposition 4.1 and set C=min⁡{C0,C1}C=\min\{C_{0},C_{1}\} as in equation 2.

If TsT_{s} is given by the Guess & Check procedure, agreeing with TtT_{t} on NN i.i.d. samples from 𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{K}, with

N≥1ϵ​(B​log⁡|𝔽|+3​log⁡(2/δ))N\geq\frac{1}{{\epsilon}}\big(B\log|\mathbb{F}|+3\log(2/\delta)\big) (44)

and

K≥|Σ|(C+log⁡(1/ϵ)+log2⁡(1/ϵ)+2​C​log⁡(1/ϵ)),K\geq|\Sigma|\left(C+\log(1/{\epsilon})+\sqrt{\log^{2}(1/{\epsilon})+2C\log(1/{\epsilon})}\right), (45)

then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the training sample and the G&C draw, we have

∀M≥K,Pr𝒟M[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)]<3ϵ.\forall M\geq K,\qquad\operatorname{Pr}_{\mathcal{D}_{M}}\left[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)\right]<3{\epsilon}. (46)
Proof.

By Proposition 4.1, the condition on NN gives, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

eK:=Prw∼𝒟K[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)]<ϵ.e_{K}:=\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{K}}[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)]<{\epsilon}.

Fix any student in this event. Its difference function’s poDFA has height at most CC by Corollaries D.1 and D.2. The condition on KK is exactly the cutoff required by Theorem D.1, which gives eM<3​ϵe_{M}<3{\epsilon} for every M≥KM\geq K. This implication is deterministic once the student is fixed, so no additional failure probability or union bound over MM is needed. ∎

Hidden dependencies.

Under the Dff=DD_{\mathrm{ff}}=D feed-forward width convention, a sufficient sample budget has order

𝒪⁡([Lt​Dt2+Ds​Dt​(Ls+Lt)+|Σ|​Ds+Ds​ν]​log⁡|𝔽|+log⁡(1/δ)ϵ).\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{[L_{t}D_{t}^{2}+D_{s}D_{t}(L_{s}+L_{t})+|\Sigma|D_{s}+D_{s}\nu]\log|\mathbb{F}|+\log(1/\delta)}{{\epsilon}}\right).

This retains the embedding and output-layer terms; the implicit constants are those of the data-complexity bound. Additionally, for ℓ=log⁡(1/ϵ)\ell=\log(1/{\epsilon}), ℓ2+2​C​ℓ≤C+ℓ\sqrt{\ell^{2}+2C\ell}\leq C+\ell, so the sufficient length cutoff from Theorem D.1 is 𝒪⁡(|Σ|​(C+log⁡(1/ϵ)))\mathcal{O}(|\Sigma|(C+\log(1/{\epsilon}))).

For ERM, the same proof applies after replacing the sample condition by the ERM condition in Proposition 4.1; the length cutoff is unchanged.

F.2 Multiplicative upper bound

We prove Theorem 4.2 from Section 4.3. For this, we importantly show that, whichever absorbing state the automaton eventually reaches, it has probability at least aC​(K)a_{C}(K) of reaching that state within KK steps. This lets us control eventual disagreement using the disagreement already visible at length KK.

Theorem F.2 (Joint generalization bound in sample size and length).

Fix s=|Σ|≥2s=|\Sigma|\geq 2, δ∈(0,15)\delta\in(0,\tfrac{1}{5}), and integers N≥1N\geq 1 and K≥0K\geq 0. Work under the learning and arithmetic assumptions of Remark 2.1 and Appendix B.2. Let TtT_{t} be the teacher and let TsT_{s} be obtained by G&C from a labeled sample S∼𝒟KNS\sim\mathcal{D}_{K}^{N}, where 𝒟K=Unif⁡(Σ≤K)\mathcal{D}_{K}=\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{\leq K}). Let BB be an admissible G&C complexity term from Proposition 4.1, let C=min⁡{C0,C1}C=\min\{C_{0},C_{1}\} be the uniform height bound in equation 43, and set

aC(K):=Pr[Bin(K,1/s)≥C],ρ:=ss−1,Bδ:=Blog|𝔽|+3log(2/δ).a_{C}(K):=\Pr[\operatorname{Bin}(K,1/s)\geq C],\qquad\rho:=\frac{s}{s-1},\qquad B_{\delta}:=B\log|\mathbb{F}|+3\log(2/\delta).

If aC​(K)>0a_{C}(K)>0, then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over SS and the G&C draw, for every integer M≥KM\geq K,

Prw∼𝒟M[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)]≤ρ​BδN​aC​(K).\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{M}}[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)]\leq\frac{\rho B_{\delta}}{N\,a_{C}(K)}. (47)

For ERM, the same statement holds with an admissible ERM complexity term B=BE​R​MB=B_{ERM} from Proposition 4.1; the probability is then only over SS.

We first establish the bound on the absorption time of an infinite run of letters.

Lemma F.1.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a reduced poDFA of height at most CC, driven by an infinite stream of i.i.d. uniform letters from Σ\Sigma. Write QnQ_{n} for its state after nn letters, TT for its first hitting time of its absorbing state, and Z=QTZ=Q_{T} the absorbing state eventually reached. Then T<∞T<\infty and for every absorbing state zz,

Pr⁡(T≤K∣Z=z)≥aC​(K).\Pr(T\leq K\mid Z=z)\geq a_{C}(K).
Proof.

At each transient state, the probability of leaving is at least 1/s1/s, so absorption must occurs within CC strict transitions. A self-loop leaves the state unchanged, and future letters are independent; thus conditioning on Z=zZ=z does not change the self-loop probability. Even under this conditioning, each step before absorption therefore makes progress with probability at least 1/s1/s. By coupling with independent Bernoulli(1/s)(1/s) trials, absorption is no slower than obtaining CC successes, giving

Pr(T≤K∣Z=z)≥Pr[Bin(K,1/s)≥C]=aC(K).\Pr(T\leq K\mid Z=z)\geq\Pr[\operatorname{Bin}(K,1/s)\geq C]=a_{C}(K).

∎

Proof of the theorem.

For a fixed student, write

pm:=Prw∼Unif⁡(Σ=m)[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)],em:=Prw∼𝒟m[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)].p_{m}:=\Pr_{w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{=m})}[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)],\qquad e_{m}:=\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{m}}[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)].

We have by convention that disagreement means a mismatch at any output position, so the difference poDFA 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} has at most a unique absorbing accepting state ⊥\bot, with its height bounded by CC.

Run 𝒜Δ\mathcal{A}_{\Delta} on an i.i.d. uniform stream, with T,ZT,Z as in the lemma, and set q∞:=Pr(Z=⊥)q_{\infty}:=\Pr(Z=\bot) the probability that the ultimate absorbing state is the disagreement one. Since ⊥\bot is absorbing,

pK=Pr(T≤K,Z=⊥)=Pr(T≤K∣Z=⊥)⋅q∞≥aC(K)⋅q∞.p_{K}=\Pr(T\leq K,\ Z=\bot)=\Pr(T\leq K\mid Z=\bot)\cdot q_{\infty}\geq a_{C}(K)\cdot q_{\infty}.

Moreover, persistence of disagreement makes pmp_{m} nondecreasing, so for every MM,

eM=∑m=0Msm​pm∑m=0Msm≤∑m=0Msm​pM∑m=0Msm=pM≤q∞.e_{M}=\frac{\sum_{m=0}^{M}s^{m}p_{m}}{\sum_{m=0}^{M}s^{m}}\leq\frac{\sum_{m=0}^{M}s^{m}p_{M}}{\sum_{m=0}^{M}s^{m}}=p_{M}\leq q_{\infty}.

To connect the exact-length quantity pKp_{K} to the training distribution, observe that

λK:=Prw∼𝒟K⁡(|w|=K)=sK∑m=0Ksm=(s−1)​sKsK+1−1>s−1s=ρ−1.\lambda_{K}:=\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{K}}(|w|=K)=\frac{s^{K}}{\sum_{m=0}^{K}s^{m}}=\frac{(s-1)s^{K}}{s^{K+1}-1}>\frac{s-1}{s}=\rho^{-1}.

Therefore eK≥λK​pK≥λK​aC​(K)​q∞e_{K}\geq\lambda_{K}p_{K}\geq\lambda_{K}a_{C}(K)q_{\infty}, which implies

eM≤q∞≤eKλK​aC​(K)≤ρ​eKaC​(K).e_{M}\leq q_{\infty}\leq\frac{e_{K}}{\lambda_{K}a_{C}(K)}\leq\frac{\rho e_{K}}{a_{C}(K)}. (48)

Finally, Proposition 4.1 gives eK≤Bδ/Ne_{K}\leq B_{\delta}/N with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, as we can apply the proposition with ϵ=Bδ/N{\epsilon}=B_{\delta}/N. Substituting into equation 48 proves the result simultaneously for every M≥KM\geq K. The ERM version is obtained identically, thanks to log⁡(1/δ)≤3​log⁡(2/δ)\log(1/\delta)\leq 3\log(2/\delta). ∎

The factor aC​(K)a_{C}(K) measures how much of the eventual disagreement is already visible at length KK and the factor ρ\rho accounts for drawing training words uniformly from all words of length at most KK.

F.3 Tradeoff between Length and Data Complexity

We give the calculations behind the tradeoff discussed in Section 4.3 and its implications for the allocation of a given token-budget. Keep the notation of Theorem F.2, with s=|Σ|≥2s=|\Sigma|\geq 2, C≥1C\geq 1, and ρ=s/(s−1)\rho=s/(s-1). Fix a target error ϵ∈(0,1){\epsilon}\in(0,1) and confidence 1−δ1-\delta. The theorem gives the sufficient sample size

Nreq​(K):=N0aC​(K),N0:=ρ​Bδϵ,K≥C.N_{\rm req}(K):=\frac{N_{0}}{a_{C}(K)},\qquad N_{0}:=\frac{\rho B_{\delta}}{{\epsilon}},\qquad K\geq C. (49)

Here N0N_{0} is the limit sample size as K→∞K\to\infty, that would still satisfy the target error ϵ{\epsilon}. Halving the target error doubles the N0N_{0}’s and so it does for Nreq​(K)N_{\rm req}(K), at every length, without changing its dependence on KK.

Three length regimes.

The following table summarizes the sample sizes certified by the bound and already discussed in Section 4.3.

training lengthsufficient number of samplesK<Cno finite N is certifiedK=CNreq​(C)=sC​N0K≥s​CN0≤Nreq​(K)≤2​N0\begin{array}[]{c|c}\text{training length}&\text{sufficient number of samples}\\ \hline\cr K<C&\text{no finite $N$ is certified}\\[2.0pt] K=C&N_{\rm req}(C)=s^{C}N_{0}\\[2.0pt] K\geq sC&N_{0}\leq N_{\rm req}(K)\leq 2N_{0}\end{array} (50)

Thus increasing length from CC to s​CsC reduces the sufficient sample size by a factor of at least sC/2s^{C}/2.

For K<CK<C, aC​(K)=0a_{C}(K)=0, while aC​(C)=s−Ca_{C}(C)=s^{-C}. At K=s​CK=sC, the binomial has integer mean CC, which is also a median (Kaas and Buhrman, 1980, Theorem 1), so aC​(s​C)≥1/2a_{C}(sC)\geq 1/2. The last row follows because aC​(K)a_{C}(K) increases to one. ∎

How to invest a fixed token budget.

Write Budget=N​K\operatorname{Budget}=NK for the token budget, an upper bound on the total number of tokens when sampling from 𝒟K\mathcal{D}_{K}. We keep KK integral and ignore rounding of NN. Substituting N=Budget/KN=\operatorname{Budget}/K into the theorem gives

Prw∼𝒟M[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)]≤ρ​BδBudgetKaC​(K)(M≥K),\Pr_{w\sim\mathcal{D}_{M}}[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)]\leq\frac{\rho B_{\delta}}{\operatorname{Budget}}\,\frac{K}{a_{C}(K)}\qquad(M\geq K), (51)

ϵ⋆​(Budget)=ρ​BδBudget​minC≤K≤Budget​KaC​(K),{\epsilon}^{\star}(\operatorname{Budget})=\frac{\rho B_{\delta}}{\operatorname{Budget}}\min_{C\leq K\leq\operatorname{Budget}}\frac{K}{a_{C}(K)},

F.4 Adaptive main theorem: uniform training length

We adapt Theorem 4.1 to the distribution that first chooses a length uniformly, then draws a word of that length:

𝒟~K:k∼Unif⁡{0,…,K},w∼Unif⁡(Σk).\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{K}:\quad k\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0,\ldots,K\},\qquad w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{k}).

The sample-size condition is unchanged. For the length transfer, we use the fact that at least half of the sampled lengths are at least K/2K/2.

Corollary F.2 (Main theorem for uniform training lengths).

Fix ϵ∈(0,12){\epsilon}\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2}), δ∈(0,15)\delta\in(0,\tfrac{1}{5}), and s=|Σ|≥2s=|\Sigma|\geq 2. Use the learning and arithmetic assumptions of Theorem F.1, with the same complexity term BB and height bound CC. Let TsT_{s} be obtained by G&C from a labeled sample S∼𝒟~KNS\sim\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{K}^{N}. If

N≥B​log⁡|𝔽|+3​log⁡(2/δ)ϵN\geq\frac{B\log|\mathbb{F}|+3\log(2/\delta)}{{\epsilon}}

and

⌈K2⌉≥s⁡(C+log⁡12​ϵ+log2⁡12​ϵ+2​C​log⁡12​ϵ),\left\lceil\frac{K}{2}\right\rceil\geq s\left(C+\log\frac{1}{2{\epsilon}}+\sqrt{\log^{2}\frac{1}{2{\epsilon}}+2C\log\frac{1}{2{\epsilon}}}\right),

∀M≥K,Prw∼𝒟~M[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)]≤4ϵ.\forall M\geq K,\qquad\Pr_{w\sim\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{M}}[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)]\leq 4{\epsilon}.

The statistical argument of Proposition 4.1 applies to any input distribution, so the condition on NN gives error at most ϵ{\epsilon} on 𝒟~K\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{K} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. Fix a student in this event and write

pm:=Prw∼Unif⁡(Σm)[Ts(w)≠Tt(w)],e~m:=1m+1∑k=0mpk.p_{m}:=\Pr_{w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{m})}[T_{s}(w)\neq T_{t}(w)],\qquad\widetilde{e}_{m}:=\frac{1}{m+1}\sum_{k=0}^{m}p_{k}.

Since I={⌈K/2⌉,…,K}I=\{\lceil K/2\rceil,\ldots,K\} contains at least half the lengths,

1|I|​∑k∈Ipk≤K+1|I|​e~K≤2​ϵ.\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{k\in I}p_{k}\leq\frac{K+1}{|I|}\widetilde{e}_{K}\leq 2{\epsilon}.

By the condition on KK and Lemma D.5, it is still transient after K~\widetilde{K} letters with probability at most 2​ϵ2{\epsilon}. Any disagreement at a later length either already occurred by K~\widetilde{K}, or the run was still transient then. Thus pm≤4​ϵp_{m}\leq 4{\epsilon} for every m>K~m>\widetilde{K}. Averaging gives, for every M≥KM\geq K,

e~M≤K+1M+1​ϵ+M−KM+1​ 4​ϵ≤4​ϵ.\widetilde{e}_{M}\leq\frac{K+1}{M+1}{\epsilon}+\frac{M-K}{M+1}\,4{\epsilon}\leq 4{\epsilon}.

This holds for all MM on the same statistical event. ∎

As usual, for ERM, use its sample-size condition from Proposition 4.1. Here, the see that the bound given on KK is roughly two times larger. However the rates do not change, and as in Theorem 4.1, the sufficient length remains 𝒪⁡(s⁡(C+log⁡(1/ϵ)))\mathcal{O}(s(C+\log(1/{\epsilon}))).

Remark F.1.

The multiplicative tradeoff bound from Theorem 4.2 also extends to 𝒟~K\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}_{K}. At least half of its mass lies on lengths between ⌈K/2⌉\lceil K/2\rceil and KK. Thus, the same averaging argument finds a length in this interval with error at most twice the average error. Repeating the proof of Theorem F.2 therefore gives a bound of order

2​BδN​aC​(⌈K/2⌉)\frac{2B_{\delta}}{N\,a_{C}(\lceil K/2\rceil)}

on every later error. The factor 22 replaces the factor ρ\rho as it represents the mass of the upper half of the length range.

Appendix G Extensions

G.1 Local Attention

We keep fixed precision and strict causal masking. Each head is either global or local; a local head at position ii attends only to max⁡(1,i−W),…,i−1\max(1,i-W),\ldots,i-1, for a common window size W≥1W\geq 1. Let Ts,TtT_{s},T_{t} have depths Ls,LtL_{s},L_{t} and the same output dimension. Set

s=|Σ|≥2,R=W​max⁡(Ls,Lt).s=|\Sigma|\geq 2,\qquad R=W\max(L_{s},L_{t}).

We consider disagreement at ordinary token positions,

Δ⁡(w)=𝟏​{∃i≤|w|:Ts​(w)i≠Tt​(w)i}.\Delta(w)=\mathbf{1}\{\exists i\leq|w|:\ T_{s}(w)_{i}\neq T_{t}(w)_{i}\}.

By causality, Δ⁡(u)=1\Delta(u)=1 implies Δ⁡(u​v)=1\Delta(uv)=1. We do not include disagreement evaluated only at EOS.

Definition G.1 (Cache–poDFA cascade).

Let suffixR⁡(u)\operatorname{suffix}_{R}(u) retain the last min⁡(R,|u|)\min(R,|u|) symbols of uu. A cache–poDFA cascade is a DFA with states (c,q)∈Σ≤R×Q(c,q)\in\Sigma^{\leq R}\times Q, initial state (ϵ,q0)({\epsilon},q_{0}), and transitions

δ⁡((c,q),a)=(suffixR⁡(c​a),f⁡(q,c,a)),q⪯f⁡(q,c,a),\delta((c,q),a)=\bigl(\operatorname{suffix}_{R}(ca),f(q,c,a)\bigr),\qquad q\preceq f(q,c,a), (54)

where (Q,⪯)(Q,\preceq) is a finite partially ordered set. Its accepting states are those with b⁡(q)=1b(q)=1, for a flag b:Q→{0,1}b:Q\to\{0,1\} satisfying b⁡(q)≤b⁡(f⁡(q,c,a))b(q)\leq b(f(q,c,a)). The ordered component is a poDFA over Σ≤R×Σ\Sigma^{\leq R}\times\Sigma: it reads the cache together with the next letter. Let Cloc≥1C_{\mathrm{loc}}\geq 1 be an integer bound on the number of strict changes of qq along a run, including a change of the disagreement flag.

Proposition G.1 (Representation of disagreement).

The language {w:Δ⁡(w)=1}\{w:\Delta(w)=1\} is recognized by a cache–poDFA cascade of radius RR. In particular, the full DFA need not be partially ordered.

Proof.

Write Yj​φY^{j}\varphi to mean that φ\varphi held jj positions earlier, with value false if that position does not exist. The finite-precision compilation of Li and Cotterell (2026) gives a pointed formula ψΔ∈LTL⁡[𝐏,Y]\psi_{\Delta}\in\mathrm{LTL}[\mathbf{P},Y] for disagreement at the current position. A local head uses the current representation and the previous WW representations, adding shifts YjY^{j} with j≤Wj\leq W. Global heads introduce only Boolean operations and 𝐏\mathbf{P}, as in Appendix C.3. Thus the total shift along any formula branch is at most RR.

Move every shift inward using

Y​𝐏​φ≡𝐏​Y​φ,Y⁡(φ∧θ)≡Y​φ∧Y​θ,Y​¬φ≡Y⊤∧¬Y​φ.Y\mathbf{P}\varphi\equiv\mathbf{P}Y\varphi,\qquad Y(\varphi\wedge\theta)\equiv Y\varphi\wedge Y\theta,\qquad Y\neg\varphi\equiv Y\top\wedge\neg Y\varphi.

Suppose tt symbols have been read, and the next symbol is a=wt+1a=w_{t+1}. For each past subformula χ=𝐏​θ\chi=\mathbf{P}\theta, store

zχ=𝟏{∃j≤t:w,j⊧θ}.z_{\chi}=\mathbf{1}\{\exists j\leq t:\ w,j\models\theta\}.

This is the truth of χ\chi before reading aa. The cache is c=suffixR(w1⋯wt)c=\operatorname{suffix}_{R}(w_{1}\cdots w_{t}).

Here d∈Σd\in\Sigma, 0≤j≤R0\leq j\leq R, and Y0Y^{0} is the identity.

zχ′=zχ∨valθ⁡(z,c,a),b′=b∨valψΔ⁡(z,c,a).z^{\prime}_{\chi}=z_{\chi}\vee\operatorname{val}_{\theta}(z,c,a),\qquad b^{\prime}=b\vee\operatorname{val}_{\psi_{\Delta}}(z,c,a).

Starting from z=b=0z=b=0, induction gives the stated meaning of zz and b=Δ(w1⋯wt)b=\Delta(w_{1}\cdots w_{t}). Each bit changes only from 00 to 11, so q=(z,b)q=(z,b) is partially ordered. Let GG count the distinct past subformulas before moving the shifts inward. Each gives at most R+1R+1 shifted versions; adding the disagreement flag gives

Cloc=(R+1)​G+1.C_{\mathrm{loc}}=(R+1)G+1. (55)

Remark G.1 (Scope of the height bound).

This construction extends the bound on the count of the past subformulas from Appendix D.1 which stems the threshold C0C_{0} in Eq. 2. Each shifted past test changes from false to true at most once, so counting these tests bounds the ordered component’s height. In particular, setting the cache window WW to 0 retrieves the global attention bound. However, we cannot extend the temporal-profile bound of Appendix D.2 with this method. Indeed, temporal profiles over Σ\Sigma do not record the recent suffix needed by local attention. Adding the cache changes the alphabet, so the original profile bound no longer applies.

Definition G.2 (Settled states and absorption).

A reachable state (c,q)(c,q) is settled if either b⁡(q)=1b(q)=1 (disagreement has occurred), or every continuation keeps b=0b=0 (disagreement is impossible). Otherwise it is transient. Merge the first kind into a bad sink and the second into a safe sink. Both sets are closed under transitions, so this preserves the language. The merged states are absorbing; let τ\tau be the first time the run reaches either of them.

Both transformers share the same suffix cache, which depends only on the input. The cache may keep changing after the outcome is settled. If the ordered component can never advance, the state is settled.

Lemma G.1 (Progress in a fresh block).

From every transient state, some word of length at most B=R+1B=R+1 strictly advances the ordered component. Consequently, for independent uniform input symbols,

Pr⁡[strict transition in the poDFA in the next ​B​ steps∣history]≥α,α=|Σ|−B.\Pr[\text{strict transition in the poDFA in the next }B\text{ steps}\mid\text{history}]\geq\alpha,\qquad\alpha=|\Sigma|^{-B}. (56)
Proof.

A transient state admits a continuation causing disagreement. Take a word vv ending at the first strict advance of the ordered component. If |v|≤B|v|\leq B, use vv. Otherwise use its final BB symbols. Either this shorter word advances the ordered component within RR steps, or those steps restore the cache just before the last symbol of vv, while qq stays fixed. The last symbol then causes the same advance. This word has length r≤Br\leq B and occurs at the start of the next block with probability s−r≥s−Bs^{-r}\geq s^{-B}, given any history. ∎

Theorem G.1 (Absorption tail with local attention).

For an i.i.d. uniform input stream, every integer K≥0K\geq 0 satisfies

Pr[τ>K]≤Pr[Bin(⌊KB⌋,α)<Cloc],B=R+1,α=s−B.\Pr[\tau>K]\leq\Pr\!\left[\operatorname{Bin}\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{K}{B}\right\rfloor,\alpha\right)<C_{\mathrm{loc}}\right],\qquad B=R+1,\quad\alpha=s^{-B}. (57)

In particular, for 0<ϵ<10<{\epsilon}<1, write ℓϵ=log⁡(1/ϵ)\ell_{\epsilon}=\log(1/{\epsilon}). The right-hand side is at most ϵ{\epsilon} whenever

K≥B⁡⌈sB​(Cloc+ℓϵ+ℓϵ2+2​Cloc​ℓϵ)⌉.K\geq B\left\lceil s^{B}\left(C_{\mathrm{loc}}+\ell_{\epsilon}+\sqrt{\ell_{\epsilon}^{2}+2C_{\mathrm{loc}}\ell_{\epsilon}}\right)\right\rceil. (58)

This gives the sufficient scale K=O⁡((R+1)​sR+1​(Cloc+log⁡(1/ϵ)))K=O\bigl((R+1)s^{R+1}(C_{\mathrm{loc}}+\log(1/{\epsilon}))\bigr).

Proof.

Split the stream into blocks of length BB. Count a block as successful if it contains an ordered advance or a settled state. By Lemma G.1, its success probability is at least α\alpha, given all previous blocks. Coupling with independent Bernoulli(α)(\alpha) trials shows that the number of successes in nn blocks stochastically dominates Bin⁡(n,α)\operatorname{Bin}(n,\alpha).

If τ>n​B\tau>nB, there are fewer than ClocC_{\mathrm{loc}} successful blocks: each contains a strict advance, and ClocC_{\mathrm{loc}} advances would leave the state settled. Taking n=⌊K/B⌋n=\lfloor K/B\rfloor proves Equation 57. For μ=⌊K/B⌋​α>Cloc\mu=\lfloor K/B\rfloor\alpha>C_{\mathrm{loc}}, the Chernoff bound gives

Pr[Bin(⌊K/B⌋,α)<Cloc]≤exp(−(μ−Cloc)22​μ).\Pr[\operatorname{Bin}(\lfloor K/B\rfloor,\alpha)<C_{\mathrm{loc}}]\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{(\mu-C_{\mathrm{loc}})^{2}}{2\mu}\right).

Condition equation 58 makes this at most ϵ{\epsilon}. ∎

Corollary G.1 (Length generalization).

Let pk=Prw∼Unif⁡(Σk)[Δ(w)=1]p_{k}=\Pr_{w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{k})}[\Delta(w)=1] and eK=Prw∼Unif⁡(Σ≤K)[Δ(w)=1]e_{K}=\Pr_{w\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\Sigma^{\leq K})}[\Delta(w)=1]. For every m≥Km\geq K,

pm≤pK+Pr[τ>K].p_{m}\leq p_{K}+\Pr[\tau>K].

Thus, if KK satisfies equation 58, then pK≤ϵp_{K}\leq{\epsilon} implies pm≤2​ϵp_{m}\leq 2{\epsilon} for all m≥Km\geq K. Likewise, eK≤ϵe_{K}\leq{\epsilon} implies pm<3​ϵp_{m}<3{\epsilon} and eM<3​ϵe_{M}<3{\epsilon} for all m,M≥Km,M\geq K.

Proof.

Couple different lengths as prefixes of one infinite stream. If a disagreement occurs after time KK but not by time KK, the state at time KK must be transient. This proves the first inequality. For bounded-length sampling,

pK≤eK/λK,λK=sK1+s+⋯+sK>s−1s≥12.p_{K}\leq e_{K}/\lambda_{K},\qquad\lambda_{K}=\frac{s^{K}}{1+s+\cdots+s^{K}}>\frac{s-1}{s}\geq\frac{1}{2}.

The tail bound gives pm<3​ϵp_{m}<3{\epsilon}; averaging the errors at lengths above KK together with eKe_{K} gives the same bound for eMe_{M}. ∎

A uniform bound on ClocC_{\mathrm{loc}} lets us combine this corollary with statistical generalization, keeping the same confidence. Local attention replaces single-step progress by blocks of length R+1R+1, with progress probability at least s−(R+1)s^{-(R+1)}.
